course.title: Engineering: Structures and Machines
course.description: Load a beam, find the forces in a truss, size a section and gear a hoist. The statics and strength of materials behind real structures.
course.audience: An adult comfortable with algebra and basic trigonometry who knows forces, Newton's laws, work and energy, as in Physics: Motion and Forces.

paragraphs: A steel beam resting on a support at each end presses down on each support with a share of its load that depends on where the load sits. It also bends, so that its top is squeezed and its bottom stretched, and it sags by an amount that can be worked out to the millimetre before the beam is ever bought. Working these things out, part by part, is how every bridge, crane and gearbox is checked before it is built, and the two subjects that do it are statics, which finds the forces on each part of a structure at rest, and strength of materials, which asks whether the part can carry them.

Most of that work is arithmetic resting on a few ideas from physics, chiefly that the forces on a body at rest add to zero and so do their turning effects. Applied with care, those ideas let you look at a roof frame and say which of its bars are being pulled and which pushed, and by how much, or look at a steel I-beam and see why its metal is gathered at the top and bottom, where bending puts it to most use.
outcomes: You'll be able to split a slanted force into parts and find the force that balances a set of forces.
You'll be able to find the reactions at the supports of a loaded beam.
You'll be able to work out the force in each member of a simple truss and say whether it is pulled or pushed.
You'll be able to turn a load into a stress, and a stress into a stretch.
You'll be able to find the speed, force and power at the output of a lever, pulley or gear train.
introduction.prerequisites: You should be comfortable with algebra and basic trigonometry, and know forces, Newton's laws, work and energy.

lessons.title: Forces as vectors

steps.headline: Forces on one line add or subtract, according to which way they point

lead.text: Begin with the simplest case, two ropes pulling a trolley along a straight rail. A force is not described by its size alone, since a pull of 6 kN to the right does something different from a pull of 6 kN to the left, so every force has *both* a size and a direction, and a quantity of that kind is called a **vector**. When two forces act along the same line they combine by ordinary arithmetic, with the direction deciding the sign.

In the figure, pull A is 6 kN to the right. If pull B adds 2 kN to the right as well, the two work together, and the **resultant**, the single force that has the same effect as both, is 8 kN to the right. If B pulls 2 kN to the left instead, it works against A and the resultant is 6 − 2, or 4 kN to the right.

afterFigure.text: Taking right as positive, the second case is +6 + (−2), so both answers come from adding signed numbers, and **the direction decides the sign**. The same bookkeeping will carry over to forces at an angle once each of them has been split into a horizontal part and a vertical part, which is the next problem.

reveal.text: The resultant keeps the direction of the larger pull. Whenever forces on one line oppose each other, the stronger side wins by exactly the difference.

steps.headline: A slanted force can be replaced by a horizontal part and a vertical part

lead.text: Return to the guy rope, which pulls on the mast with 8 kN along a line at 45° to the ground. That direction is neither along the ground nor along the mast, so neither of the one-line rules applies directly. What does work is to replace the single slanted force by two forces at right angles to each other, one horizontal and one vertical, that together have *exactly* the same effect. These two forces are the **components** of the original.

The force and its components form a right-angled triangle, with the force as the sloping side. If θ is the angle between the force and the horizontal, the side that touches the angle is the **horizontal component, F cos θ**, and the side opposite the angle is the **vertical component, F sin θ**. For 8 kN at 45° both are 8 × 0.7071, which is 5.66 kN, so the rope pulls the mast sideways with 5.66 kN and presses it into the ground with 5.66 kN. At 30° the triangle is flatter, and the horizontal share grows to 6.93 kN while the vertical share falls to 4.00 kN.

afterFigure.text: Two checks are worth making every time. A component can never be larger than the force it comes from, and the shares must agree with the picture, because a flat force is mostly horizontal and a steep one mostly vertical. The usual slip is to swap sine and cosine, and the picture catches it, since the side that touches the angle is the one that takes the cosine.

steps.headline: Splitting a 20 kN force at 60° into its components

lead.text: A cable pulls on a fixing with 20 kN at 60° above the horizontal. Keep the calculator in degrees mode.

workedSteps.text: Draw the force as the sloping side of a right-angled triangle, with θ = 60° between it and the horizontal.
The horizontal side touches the angle, so it takes the cosine.
The vertical side is opposite the angle, so it takes the sine.
As a check, the two parts must rebuild the force. Squaring and adding them gives back 20².

steps.headline: A slope triangle gives the components without a calculator

lead.text: Drawings often give the direction of a force as a slope instead of an angle, such as a brace that rises 3 m for every 4 m across. The slope makes a right-angled **slope triangle** with a rise of 3, a run of 4 and a sloping side of √(3² + 4²), which is 5. The force and its [[components|The two parts, at right angles, that together replace a force. Met in 'A slanted force can be replaced by a horizontal part and a vertical part'.]] are in the same proportion as the sides of that triangle, so **the components are the force multiplied by run over length and by rise over length**.

In the figure, a 30 kN force along the 3-in-4 slope has a horizontal component of 30 × 4/5 = 24 kN and a vertical component of 30 × 3/5 = 18 kN. The second case is a 34 kN force on a slope that rises 8 for every 15 across, where the sloping side is √(8² + 15²) = √289 = 17, so the shares are 15/17 and 8/17 and the components are 30 kN and 16 kN.

afterFigure.text: Triangles with whole-number sides, such as 3–4–5 and 8–15–17, are convenient because they make the arithmetic clean, but any slope works, since only the *proportions* of the sides matter. Both routes, the angle and the slope, lead to the same two numbers.

steps.headline: Finding the vertical component of 15 kN on a 3-in-4 slope

lead.text: The first two lines set the triangle up and the last one is yours.

workedSteps.text: The slope rises 3 for every 4 across, so the sloping side is 5 and the triangle is 3–4–5.
The vertical side is the rise, so the vertical share of the force is the rise over the sloping side.
Multiply the 15 kN force by that share and give the vertical component in kN.

steps.headline: Forces at right angles combine by Pythagoras, not by addition

lead.text: Once every slanted force has been split, the [[components|The two parts, at right angles, that together replace a force. Met in 'A slanted force can be replaced by a horizontal part and a vertical part'.]] can be added direction by direction, and what is left is one horizontal force and one vertical force acting at the same point. Those two cannot be added as numbers. A horizontal pull of 20 kN and a vertical pull of 21 kN do not make a pull of 41 kN, because 41 kN is what the same two pulls would give if they acted along one line. Simon Stevin published the rule for combining forces at a point as the diagonal of a parallelogram in 1586, and Newton gave it again in the *Principia* of 1687.

The [[resultant|The single force that has the same effect as several forces together. Met in 'Forces on one line add or subtract, according to which way they point'.]] of the two is the long side of the right-angled triangle whose other sides are the forces. By Pythagoras its size is **√(20² + 21²) = √841 = 29 kN**, and it points at arctan(21 ÷ 20), about 46°, above the horizontal. It is always larger than either force and smaller than their sum, and it reaches the sum only when the forces point the same way, as the second case shows.

afterFigure.text: This gives the whole procedure for any number of forces: **split each force, add the components in each direction, and combine the two totals** by Pythagoras. The totals carry signs, so a component that points left or down counts against one that points right or up.

steps.headline: A free-body diagram shows one body and every force acting on it

lead.text: To find an unknown force, decide first which body the question is about, and then draw that body alone with an arrow for every force that acts *on* it. A sketch of this kind is a **free-body diagram**. The figure shows one for a lamp hung from two cables: the lamp is pulled down by its weight and pulled up and outward by each cable. The ceiling is missing, because its weight acts on the ceiling, and so is the lamp's pull on the cables, because that force acts on the cables.

afterFigure.text: A body at rest is in **equilibrium**, which means the [[resultant|The single force that has the same effect as several forces together. Met in 'Forces on one line add or subtract, according to which way they point'.]] of the forces on it is zero. That gives the working rule of this lesson: when every force but one is known, **the unknown force is equal in size to the resultant of the others and opposite in direction**. For the lamp, the vertical parts of the two cable pulls together equal its weight, while their horizontal parts cancel each other, and the arrows in the diagram are drawn to that scale.

blocks.text: A guy rope runs from the top of a mast to a peg in the ground, and it pulls on the mast with a force of 8 kN along a line at 45° to the ground. The 8 kN describes the rope, but it is not what the mast feels: one part of the pull tries to push the mast sideways, another part presses it into the ground, and the foundation has to be designed for each part separately.

Splitting a slanted force into parts along two chosen directions, and adding such parts back together, is the first skill of structural engineering. Every later calculation in this course, for beams, trusses and cables, begins with the forces on a body written in that form.

recap.keyIdea: A slanted force can be replaced by a horizontal and a vertical component, and forces at a point are in balance when their resultant is zero.

blocks.text: A slanted force can be replaced by two [[components|The two parts, at right angles, that together replace a force. Met in 'A slanted force can be replaced by a horizontal part and a vertical part'.]] at right angles, **F cos θ** along the side that touches the angle and **F sin θ** along the side opposite it, or by the proportions of a slope triangle when the direction is given as a slope. Components in the same direction add with their signs, and the two totals combine as the sides of a right-angled triangle, so the size of the [[resultant|The single force that has the same effect as several forces together. Met in 'Forces on one line add or subtract, according to which way they point'.]] is the square root of the two totals squared and added, and *not* their sum.

A body at rest is in **equilibrium**, so its forces have a resultant of zero, and an unknown force balances the others when it is equal to their resultant in size and opposite in direction. The free-body diagram, which shows only the forces acting on the body, is where each of these calculations starts.

recap.nextHook: A force that acts away from a pivot also turns the body, and the next lesson measures that turning effect.

lessons.title: Turning effect: moments

steps.headline: The moment of a force is the force times its distance from the pivot

lead.text: A force applied away from a fixed point tends to turn the body about that point, and the quantity that measures the tendency is the **moment** of the force. For a push at right angles to a spanner it is the size of the push multiplied by its distance from the bolt, the fixed point about which the spanner turns, which is called the **pivot**. Physics courses call the same quantity torque.

A force is measured in newtons and a distance in metres, so a moment is measured in newton metres, written N·m. In the figure, a 100 N push at right angles to the spanner, 0.2 m from the pivot, has a moment of 100 × 0.2 = 20 N·m. The same push applied twice as far out, at 0.4 m, has *twice* the moment, 40 N·m, which is why a longer handle turns a stubborn nut with less effort.

afterFigure.text: A moment is not a force, so it can never be added to one. A moment of 40 N·m says how strongly something turns, and it can come from a small force acting far from the pivot or from a large one acting close to it, which is exactly the trade that a lever makes.

steps.headline: Only the part of a force across the spanner turns it

lead.text: So far every push has been at right angles to the spanner. A push at a slant has two [[components|The two parts, at right angles, that together replace a force. Met in 'Forces as vectors'.]], one along the handle and one across it. The part along the handle presses straight on the bolt, or pulls straight away from it, and cannot turn the spanner, so only the part across the handle counts. If θ is the angle between the push and the spanner, the part across is F sin θ, and **the moment is F sin θ multiplied by the distance d** from the pivot.

In the figure, 100 N at right angles to a spanner 0.4 m long has a moment of 100 × 0.4 = 40 N·m. The same 100 N tilted to 60° to the handle has an across-part of 100 sin 60° = 86.6 N, so its moment falls to 86.6 × 0.4 = 34.64 N·m. The tilt has wasted part of the push, and a force of a given size has its largest moment when it is at right angles to the spanner.

steps.headline: The perpendicular distance to the line of action does the same job

lead.text: There is a second way to reach the same result. Extend the arrow of a force in both directions into a long dashed line, which is the force's **line of action**, and measure from the pivot to that line by the shortest route, which meets it at a right angle. That length is the **perpendicular distance**, and the moment is the force *times* the perpendicular distance.

afterFigure.text: For the push at 60°, the perpendicular distance is 0.4 × sin 60° = 0.346 m, so the moment is 100 × 0.346 = 34.64 N·m, the same as before. The two methods are one calculation grouped in two ways, F sin θ × d against F × (d sin θ), and the second is easier whenever a drawing shows where the line of action lies. It also shows that **sliding a force along its own line of action does not change its moment**, because the perpendicular distance stays the same.

steps.headline: Finding the moment of 80 N at 40° on a spanner 0.35 m long

lead.text: A mechanic pushes a spanner with 80 N at 40° to the handle, at a point 0.35 m from the bolt.

workedSteps.text: Only the part of the push across the handle turns the bolt, and it is the force times the sine of the angle to the handle.
Work out the force across the spanner.
Multiply that force by its distance from the bolt.
As a check, the perpendicular distance from the bolt to the line of action is 0.35 sin 40° = 0.225 m, and the force times that gives the same moment.

reveal.text: The 200 N pull still loads the bolt, but it has no turning effect on it. A force whose line of action passes through the pivot has a moment of zero about it.

steps.headline: A body balances when the clockwise moments equal the anticlockwise ones

lead.text: A moment can turn a body in either of two senses, **clockwise** or **anticlockwise**, and engineers give one of them a plus sign and the other a minus sign so that they can be added. A see-saw shows what happens when the two senses meet. In the figure, a 200 N child sits 1.5 m to the left of the pivot, which gives an anticlockwise moment of 200 × 1.5 = 300 N·m, and a 300 N child sits 1 m to the right, which gives a clockwise moment of 300 × 1 = 300 N·m. The two are equal, so the see-saw stays level.

Move the heavier child to 1.5 m and the clockwise moment grows to 300 × 1.5 = 450 N·m, which is 150 N·m more than the anticlockwise one, and that difference is the net moment that tips the see-saw clockwise.

afterFigure.text: Archimedes proved the law of the lever in the third century BC, and in these terms it says that **a body at rest has zero net moment about any point**. The heavier child balances the lighter one by sitting nearer the pivot, in inverse proportion to the weights, and the same rule will find the forces that hold up a beam in the next lesson.

reveal.text: Because the push is at 30°, the mechanic must push twice as hard as for a right-angled push. Changing the angle changes the force needed, even though the moment on the nut is the same.

lessons.orientation: Find the moment of a force about a pivot, including a force at a slant, and balance clockwise moments against anticlockwise ones.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A tight wheel nut will not turn when you push on a short spanner, yet it gives way on a spanner twice as long, with exactly the same push. The force on the handle has not changed, and what has changed is how far from the nut it is applied. A force acting on a body away from a fixed point does more than push it, because it also tends to turn it, and how strongly it turns depends on the distance as well as on the size of the force.

Engineers need that turning effect for everything that turns on a hinge or an axle, from a door to a crane arm, and above all for beams, whose supports have to balance the loads on them in the same way. Once it is measured as a single number, the turning effect of one force can be set against that of another, which tells you how hard to push on a spanner to free a nut and where a load has to sit for a beam to stay level.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the moment of a force about a pivot, even a slanted one, and balance clockwise moments against anticlockwise ones.
intro.whyItMatters: Every support force on a beam in the next lesson is found by balancing moments.

recap.keyIdea: The moment of a force about a pivot is the force times its perpendicular distance from the pivot, and a body at rest has equal clockwise and anticlockwise moments.

blocks.text: The [[moment|The turning effect of a force about a point: the force times its perpendicular distance from the point, in N·m. Met in 'The moment of a force is the force times its distance from the pivot'.]] of a force about a pivot is **the force times the perpendicular distance from the pivot to its line of action**, in N·m. A push at right angles to the spanner uses the distance along the spanner, a slanted push uses only its across-part, F sin θ, and a force whose line of action passes through the pivot has no moment at all.

A body at rest has *no* net moment about any point, so its clockwise moments equal its anticlockwise ones. That equality is what lets an unknown force be found from the known ones, as the heavier child on a see-saw is placed from the weights alone.

recap.nextHook: Choosing the pivot at one support of a beam removes that support's force from the equation, and the next lesson uses that to find the forces holding a beam up.

lessons.title: Reactions of a supported beam

steps.headline: A support pushes back on the beam with a reaction

lead.text: Every support holds a beam up by pushing on it, and the force with which it does so is called a **reaction**. It needs a name of its own because, unlike a load, it is not given in advance: the load is known, while the reaction is whatever the support has to supply for the beam to stay at rest.

Two kinds of support are used in this lesson. A **pin** holds the beam in place both vertically and horizontally but lets it turn, like the axle of a hinge, while a **roller** resists only vertical movement, so the beam can slide along it and turn on it. A beam is usually pinned at one end and rested on a roller at the other, so that it can lengthen as it warms without pushing its supports apart. A fixed support, such as a wall that grips a cantilever, stops the turning as well and is met later in the course.

afterFigure.text: In the figure, an 18 kN load at the middle of an 8 m beam is shared equally, 9 kN at each support. Moved to 6 m from the left support, the load is nearer the right-hand support, which now takes 13.5 kN while the left takes only 4.5 kN. In both cases the two reactions add up to the 18 kN load, which is the first of two conditions that the next screen uses to find them.

reveal.text: Supports are named for what they allow. A roller lets the beam slide and turn, a pin lets it turn but not slide, and a fixed support lets it do neither.

steps.headline: Taking moments about one support leaves a single unknown force

lead.text: A beam at rest is in [[equilibrium|The state of a body at rest, in which the resultant of the forces on it is zero. Met in 'Forces as vectors'.]], so the forces on it have no resultant and the [[moments|The turning effects of forces about a point: force times perpendicular distance. Met in 'Turning effect: moments'.]] about any point add to zero. With two unknown reactions, RA at the pin A and RB at the roller B, those two conditions give two equations, and the skill lies in choosing the point about which to take moments. If that point is the support A itself, the reaction RA has no distance from it and so has no moment, and **only RB is left in the equation**.

Take the 8 m beam with a 16 kN load 3 m from A. About A, the load turns the beam clockwise with a moment of 16 × 3 = 48 kN·m, and RB turns it anticlockwise with a moment of RB × 8. The two are equal, so RB = 48 ÷ 8 = 6 kN. The vertical forces must also add to zero, so RA + RB = 16 and RA = 16 − 6 = 10 kN. Moments about B give the same answer for RA directly, since 10 × 8 = 16 × 5.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the load at 3 m and then at 5 m, and the two reactions swap. **The support nearer the load carries more of it**, in proportion to how close the load is, and the two reactions together always carry the whole load.

steps.headline: Finding both reactions for 18 kN at 3 m and 9 kN at 6 m on a 9 m beam

lead.text: A 9 m beam has a pin at A and a roller at B, one at each end. It carries 18 kN at 3 m from A and 9 kN at 6 m from A.

workedSteps.text: Take moments about A, so that RA drops out. The two loads turn the beam clockwise and RB turns it anticlockwise, and the two sides are equal.
Work out the right-hand side, then divide by the span.
The vertical forces add to zero, so RA is whatever remains of the 27 kN of load.
As a check, take moments about B instead and compare.

steps.headline: Finding the reaction at B for 12 kN at 2 m on a 6 m beam

lead.text: The beam has a pin at A and a roller at B, 6 m apart. The first lines are set out and the last one is yours.

workedSteps.text: Take moments about A, so that RA drops out and RB is the only unknown.
workedSteps.math: RB × span = load × its distance from A

workedSteps.text: Put in the numbers: the span is 6 m, and the 12 kN load is 2 m from A.
Solve for RB and give it in kN.

steps.headline: A spread load acts as one force at the middle of its length

lead.text: Not every load is concentrated at a point. The weight of a deck, snow on a roof or water in a channel is **spread** over a length of beam, and its size is given per metre, as in 2 kN/m. Over a length L the whole spread load is w × L, where w is the load per metre, and for finding reactions it can be replaced by **a single force of that size acting at the middle of the loaded length**, because a uniform load has its centre there.

In the figure, 2 kN/m spread over the first 4 m of an 8 m beam is a total of 2 × 4 = 8 kN acting 2 m from A. Moments about A give RB × 8 = 8 × 2, so RB = 2 kN and RA = 8 − 2 = 6 kN. The second case replaces the spread load by a single 8 kN load at 2 m, and the reactions come out exactly the same, which is what the replacement means.

afterFigure.text: The replacement is for finding the reactions only. Inside the beam the load is still spread out along its length, and the lessons on shear and bending look at what that does to the material.

steps.headline: A load beyond a support can make the other support pull down

lead.text: The supports of a beam need not be at its ends. A beam that extends past a support has an **overhang**, and a load on the overhang acts on the far side of that support, so it tends to turn the beam the other way about it. In the first case of the figure the supports are at 0 and 6 m, the beam runs out to 8 m, and a 9 kN load hangs at the end of the overhang. Moments about A give RB × 6 = 9 × 8 = 72, so RB = 12 kN, which is *more* than the load. The vertical forces still add to zero, so RA = 9 − 12 = −3 kN.

With upward taken as positive, the minus sign means that the left support pulls the beam down with 3 kN, as a bolt or a heavy anchor would have to, because the load on the overhang tries to lever the beam up at A about B. Move the load between the supports, as in the second case, and both reactions are upward again, 4.5 kN each.

reveal.text: Any mix of loads reduces to single forces in the same way, and one moment equation about a support then gives the other support's reaction.

lessons.orientation: Find the support reactions of a beam by taking moments about a support and balancing the vertical forces.

blocks.text: A steel beam 8 m long rests on a support at each end, with an 18 kN load somewhere along it. At the middle, the load is shared equally between the two supports, but moved towards one end it is carried mostly by the nearer one, and each support has to be built for the share that it actually receives. The beam looks the same in both cases, and what differs is the pair of upward forces that the supports exert on it.

Finding those forces is the first step in the design of any beam, because a beam cannot be checked for bending until the forces on it are known. Two ideas from the last two lessons are enough: the forces on a beam at rest add to zero, and so do their moments.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the support forces of a loaded beam by taking moments about a support and balancing the vertical forces.
intro.whyItMatters: Every beam check later in the course starts from its support forces.

recap.keyIdea: A beam at rest has vertical forces and moments that each add to zero, and taking moments about one support gives the reaction at the other.

blocks.text: The [[reaction|The force a support exerts on a beam to hold it up. Met in 'A support pushes back on the beam with a reaction'.]] at a support is the force it exerts to hold the beam at rest, and it is found from the two conditions of equilibrium: the vertical forces add to zero, and the moments about any point add to zero. **Taking moments about one support removes its reaction from the equation**, which leaves the other one alone, and a spread load can be replaced by a single force at the middle of its length for this purpose.

A reaction can be *negative*, since a load beyond a support may force the other support to pull the beam down. Whatever the loading, the two reactions together carry the whole load, which gives a quick check on every answer.

recap.nextHook: A balance of forces applied one joint at a time, in the same way, gives the force in every bar of a truss.

lessons.title: Trusses: the method of joints

steps.headline: A member is pulled or pushed along its own length

lead.text: A **truss** is a frame of straight bars, called **members**, pinned together at their ends, which are called **joints**, with the loads applied at the joints. Because a pin lets a member turn freely, nothing can bend a member sideways, and the only force it can carry is a pull or a push *along* its own length. Timber roofs and bridges were built as trusses long before they were analysed: Andrea Palladio drew truss bridges in 1570, and the American engineer Squire Whipple published a method for calculating the forces in a truss in 1847.

A member that is stretched is in **tension** and pulls on the joints at its ends, while a member that is squeezed is in **compression** and pushes on them. A rope can work only in tension, and a short strut mainly in compression, and the figure shows the arrows that each of them exerts on its joints.

afterFigure.text: Every truss is built from triangles, because three bars joined in a triangle cannot change shape without one of the bars changing length, whereas a frame of four bars folds up into a parallelogram. The question for each bar is how much force it carries, and whether it is pulled or pushed.

reveal.text: The two names describe the force that the member exerts on its joints. A member pulling the joints together is in tension, and a member pushing them apart is in compression.

steps.headline: Isolating one joint turns a truss into a problem of forces at a point

lead.text: To find the force in each member, imagine cutting round one joint and drawing it alone as a [[free-body diagram|A sketch of one body alone with every force acting on it. Met in 'Forces as vectors'.]]. What remains is a set of forces acting at a single point: the load or reaction at the joint, and one force along each member that meets it. Those forces are in [[equilibrium|The state of a body at rest, in which the resultant of the forces on it is zero. Met in 'Forces as vectors'.]], so **the horizontal forces add to zero and the vertical forces add to zero**.

Start at the joint where the fewest members meet. In the triangular frame in the figure, a load W hangs at the apex C, and only the members AC and BC meet there. The frame is symmetrical, so they carry the same force F, and each pushes on C up and outward at the angle θ that the member makes with the horizontal. The outward parts cancel, and the two vertical parts, each F sin θ, carry the load, so **2F sin θ = W**.

afterFigure.text: Since sin θ is the rise of a member divided by its length, F = W ÷ (2 sin θ), and a flatter frame gives a larger force in its members. The two members push upward on C to hold the load up, so each is pushed along its length and is in compression.

steps.headline: The bottom member holds the feet of the frame together

lead.text: Move on to joint A. Its forces are the support's reaction, pushing up with half of the load by symmetry, the sloping member AC, pushing on the joint down and outward, and the bottom member AB. The reaction exactly balances the vertical part of AC, which checks the apex calculation, and that leaves the horizontal forces: the outward push of AC has to be cancelled by AB, so **AB pulls the foot back towards B** and is in tension.

The first case of the figure has a load of 36 kN on a frame 8 m wide and 3 m high, with sloping members 5 m long. Each foot carries a reaction of 18 kN, so a sloping member has 18 ÷ (3/5) = 30 kN in compression, and the bottom member has 30 × 4/5 = 24 kN in tension. In the second case the frame is narrower and steeper, 6 m wide and 4 m high, and the same load gives smaller forces, 22.5 kN in each sloping member and 13.5 kN in the bottom one.

afterFigure.text: Without its bottom member, the feet of the frame would slide apart on the roller, so AB does the work that the support cannot do. It is also why the tension in AB, and the compression in the sloping members, grow as the frame is made flatter.

steps.headline: Finding every member force for 10 kN on a 12 m roof truss

lead.text: A symmetrical roof truss spans 12 m, with its apex 2.5 m above the supports, so each sloping member is 6.5 m long. A 10 kN load hangs at the apex.

workedSteps.text: The truss is symmetrical, so the two supports share the load equally.
At the apex C, the vertical parts of the two sloping members, each F × 2.5/6.5, together carry the load.
Solve for F. The members push up on C, so they are in compression.
At the foot A, the bottom member balances the horizontal part of the sloping member, which is its force times run over length. It pulls on the joint, so it is in tension.
As a check, the vertical forces at A must balance, so the reaction equals the vertical part of the sloping member.

steps.headline: Finding the force in the bottom member from the force in a sloping one

lead.text: Joint A is isolated, and the first two lines set the balance out. The last one is yours.

workedSteps.text: The sloping member pushes on joint A down and outward. Its horizontal part is its force times run over length, with a run of 2 m and a length of 2.5 m.
The bottom member must cancel that horizontal part, so its force is equal to it.
Work it out, and give the force in AB in kN.

steps.headline: A joint with no load and two members in line leaves the third member with no force

lead.text: Some members carry no force at all, and spotting them saves a joint of arithmetic. Look at the joint in the figure, where members P and Q lie along one horizontal line and member R leaves at an angle. Take the vertical forces there. P and Q are horizontal, so neither has a vertical part, and with no load at the joint the only force with a vertical part is R. It has nothing to balance, so **R must carry no force**.

Hang a load from the joint, as in the second case, and R has a load to help carry, so it is no longer zero. The rule therefore holds only when the joint carries no load. A member of this kind is called a **zero-force member**. It still has a job, since it keeps the frame stable and takes force if the loading changes, but it can be left out of the calculation for the loading given.

blocks.text: Three bars pinned together at their ends make a triangle, and a triangle is the one shape that cannot be pushed out of shape without changing the length of a bar. That is why roofs, cranes and bridges are built from frames of bars joined in triangles. When a load hangs from the top of a simple triangular frame, its two sloping bars are squeezed while the bar across the bottom is stretched, and a timber roof and a steel bridge are doing the same thing.

Each bar carries a different force, and that force has to be known before the bar can be sized. All of them can be found using nothing beyond the balance of forces at a point from the first lesson of the course.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the force in each bar of a simple truss, joint by joint, and say whether each bar is pulled or pushed.
intro.whyItMatters: A bar sized for the wrong force either fails or wastes steel.

recap.keyIdea: The method of joints balances the horizontal and vertical forces at one joint at a time, giving the force in each member and whether it is pulled or pushed.

blocks.text: The method of joints isolates one joint at a time, beginning where only two unknown members meet, and balances the horizontal and the vertical forces on it. At the apex of a symmetrical triangle the two sloping members share the load and are in [[compression|A member that is squeezed and pushes on the joints at its ends. Met in 'A member is pulled or pushed along its own length'.]], each carrying W ÷ (2 sin θ), and at each foot **the bottom member balances the horizontal part** of the sloping one and is in [[tension|A member that is stretched and pulls on the joints at its ends. Met in 'A member is pulled or pushed along its own length'.]].

A joint with no load, where two members lie along one line, leaves the third member with *no* force, and recognising such a zero-force member saves a joint of arithmetic. Because every joint must balance, the result can always be checked by returning to a joint already solved.

lessons.title: Stress, strain and stiffness

steps.headline: Stress is the force on each square millimetre of a cross-section

lead.text: Suppose a steel rod carries an axial pull of 24 kN, that is, a pull along its length. Whether it survives depends on how much steel carries the pull, because the same 24 kN is easy for a thick rod and fatal to a thin wire. The measure that matters is the force on each square millimetre of the rod's cross-section, the cut across its width, which is called **stress** and written σ (sigma): **σ = F ÷ A**, with F the force and A the cross-sectional area.

With the force in newtons and the area in square millimetres, stress comes out in N/mm², which is called a **megapascal**, or MPa, because a pascal is a newton on a square metre and a square metre is a million square millimetres. Loads are usually quoted in kN, so **convert to newtons first**: 24 kN is 24,000 N.

afterFigure.text: On a rod of 200 mm², which is about 16 mm across, the 24 kN gives 24,000 ÷ 200 = 120 MPa, while on a rod with three times the area it gives 24,000 ÷ 600 = 40 MPa. Tripling the area cuts the stress to a third, and the same happens when identical rods share a load, since each carries the total divided by the number of rods.

steps.headline: Strain is the stretch as a fraction of the original length

lead.text: Stress says how hard the material is loaded, and the matching measure of how far it stretches is strain. A rod 5,000 mm long that stretches by 4 mm has not stretched much, while a rod 500 mm long that stretches by the same 4 mm has stretched ten times as much for its size, so the useful quantity is the extension divided by the original length. That ratio is the **strain**, written ε (epsilon): **ε = δ ÷ L**, where δ (delta) is the extension and L is the original length, both in the same unit.

afterFigure.text: For this rod, 4 ÷ 5,000 = 0.0008. Strain has no unit, because it is one length divided by another, and strains in structures are tiny, typically a fraction of one percent, which is why a loaded steel member does not visibly stretch.

steps.headline: Young's modulus ties stress to strain

lead.text: Within a certain range, stress and strain rise together in proportion, so doubling the load doubles the stretch. Robert Hooke published this proportionality in 1678, and the constant that connects the two is a property of the material, called **Young's modulus** after Thomas Young, who described it in 1807, and written E. It makes **σ = E × ε**. Strain has no unit, so E has the unit of stress, and it is large: structural steel has an E of about 200 GPa, which is 200,000 MPa, and aluminium alloys about 70 GPa.

In the figure, a 16 kN pull on a rod of 400 mm² and 1,000 mm long gives a stress of 16,000 ÷ 400 = 40 MPa, whatever the metal. For steel the strain is 40 ÷ 200,000 = 0.0002 and the rod stretches by 0.2 mm, while for aluminium the strain is 40 ÷ 70,000 = 0.00057 and the rod stretches by 0.57 mm, almost three times as much. The aluminium is no weaker under this load; it is *less stiff*.

steps.headline: Beyond the yield stress a rod keeps part of its stretch

lead.text: The proportion between stress and strain does not go on for ever. Up to the **yield stress** the rod is **elastic**, which means that it returns exactly to its original length when the load is taken away. Beyond the yield stress it becomes **plastic**, which means that part of the stretch stays when the load is removed. Mild steel shows this plainly: its stress–strain curve is a straight line up to the yield stress, then flattens as the steel yields, rises again as it hardens up to its **ultimate strength**, and finally the rod thins at one point and fractures.

In the first case of the figure, 100 kN on 400 mm² is 250 MPa, below the yield stress of 355 MPa, so the strain is 250 ÷ 200,000 = 0.00125 and the 2,400 mm rod stretches by 3 mm, all of which comes back. In the second case, 160 kN gives 400 MPa, above the yield stress and below the ultimate strength of 510 MPa: the rod survives but is stretched for good, and the straight-line formula no longer says by how much.

reveal.text: A bar that has yielded does not return to its old length, and it also behaves differently on the next loading, so a structure is normally designed to stay below the yield stress.
The 180 MPa in each aluminium rod is a stress the metal carries comfortably, and the stretch of 3.6 mm is small against 1,400 mm of length, as an elastic strain should be.

blocks.text: A rod of mild steel 5 m long and 20 mm across hangs from a roof beam. Under a load of 30 kN it stretches by about 2.4 mm, too little to see, and it returns to its exact length when the load is taken off. Under 90 kN it stretches by much more than three times as much, and part of that stretch never comes back.

The load alone cannot predict this, because a thicker rod would carry 90 kN without harm. What matters is how much steel shares the load, and once the load on each square millimetre of the rod is known, together with how stiff the steel is, you can work out how far a rod of any size will stretch and whether the stretch will come back when the load is removed.

recap.keyIdea: Stress is force per area and strain is stretch per length, and in the elastic range Young's modulus connects them.

blocks.text: The [[stress|The force on each square millimetre of a cross-section, in MPa. Met in 'Stress is the force on each square millimetre of a cross-section'.]] in a rod is the force divided by the cross-sectional area, **σ = F ÷ A**, and the [[strain|The stretch as a fraction of the original length, with no unit. Met in 'Strain is the stretch as a fraction of the original length'.]] is the stretch divided by the original length, **ε = δ ÷ L**. In the elastic range the two are proportional, [[Young's modulus|The stress that goes with a strain of one in the elastic range, E, a property of the material. Met in 'Young's modulus ties stress to strain'.]] being the constant, so **δ = (σ ÷ E) × L**, with E written in MPa to match the stress.

Below the [[yield stress|The stress at which a material stops being elastic and starts to stretch for good. Met in 'Beyond the yield stress a rod keeps part of its stretch'.]] the stretch is *elastic* and disappears when the load does, and above it part of the stretch stays for good. A load is converted to newtons before dividing by an area in square millimetres, and identical members share a load equally, so each carries the total divided by their number.

lessons.title: Factor of safety and sizing

steps.headline: A factor of safety is how many times stronger a member is than its load requires

lead.text: A member is designed so that it could carry far more than it ever will. The ratio between the load that would make it fail and the load it is meant to carry is called the **factor of safety**, and for the chain in the opening it is 150 ÷ 50 = 3.

The reserve is needed because nothing in an engineering calculation is known exactly. The loads are estimates, and the real ones may be larger or may act in ways nobody allowed for; the steel supplied may be a little weaker than its specification, a bar may be a little thinner than drawn, and a weld may be worse than the test piece. The Quebec Bridge collapsed while it was being built, in 1907, after the weight of its own steelwork had been underestimated, which shows what a reserve has to cover.

How large the factor should be is a matter of judgement and of design codes, higher where failure would endanger lives or where the loads are uncertain, lower where they are well known. Here the factor is taken as given, and the lesson shows how it decides the size of a member.

reveal.text: A factor of safety is always capacity divided by demand, so it is more than one for a member that is safe, and a value below one would mean that the member fails.

steps.headline: In terms of stress, the factor of safety compares the working stress with the yield stress

lead.text: Engineers usually apply the factor to stress rather than to load, because the stress at which steel starts to yield is a property of the steel and does not depend on the size of the member. The [[stress|The force on each square millimetre of a cross-section, in MPa. Met in 'Stress, strain and stiffness'.]] that a member carries under its normal load is its **working stress**, and the factor of safety against yield is **the yield stress divided by the working stress**. A member working at exactly its [[yield stress|The stress at which steel stops being elastic and starts to stretch for good. Met in 'Stress, strain and stiffness'.]] has a factor of one, which means no margin at all.

In the figure, a steel that yields at 360 MPa is loaded with 24 kN on a rod of 200 mm². The working stress is 24,000 ÷ 200 = 120 MPa, so the factor of safety is 360 ÷ 120 = 3. Doubling the load to 48 kN doubles the working stress to 240 MPa and halves the factor to 360 ÷ 240 = 1.5.

afterFigure.text: The factor falls as the load rises or as the area shrinks, and it is the factor, not the stress alone, that tells the designer how much margin is left.

steps.headline: Turning the factor around gives the allowable stress and the area a load needs

lead.text: Design runs the calculation the other way round. The factor of safety is chosen first, and the largest stress that the member may be allowed to carry follows from it: the **allowable stress** is the yield stress divided by the factor of safety. Steel that yields at 300 MPa, designed with a factor of 2.5, may be worked to 300 ÷ 2.5 = 120 MPa and no further. Since stress is force divided by area, **the smallest area that keeps the stress at or below the allowable value is the force divided by the allowable stress**. For a tie carrying 48 kN in that steel the area is 48,000 ÷ 120 = 400 mm², with the force in newtons so that the area comes out in square millimetres.

Bars come only in standard sizes, so the area found is a *minimum*. The bar chosen is the smallest stock size whose area is at least that minimum, which means rounding up and never down, because a bar below the minimum would be working above its allowable stress.

steps.headline: A member that is strong enough must also be stiff enough

lead.text: Strength is only one of two checks. A tie can stay well below its yield stress and still stretch more than the structure around it can tolerate, because the stretch depends on the area and on the modulus, and not on the yield stress. After a bar has been chosen for strength, its stretch, **δ = (σ ÷ E) × L**, is worked out and compared with whatever limit the design allows.

The figure shows 20 kN carried by a steel tie 3 m long, first as a 12 mm square bar and then as a 16 mm square one. The 12 mm bar has an area of 144 mm², a working stress of 138.9 MPa, a factor of safety of only 1.8 against a yield stress of 250 MPa, and a stretch of 2.08 mm. The 16 mm bar has 256 mm², a stress of 78.1 MPa, a factor of 3.2, and a stretch of 1.17 mm.

afterFigure.text: A thicker bar improves both measures at once, because the area sits underneath the force in the stress and so in the stretch as well. The designer therefore sizes for strength with the allowable stress, and then checks the stretch of the bar that was chosen.

The unused strength looks like waste, but it is all that stands between a calculation and the real world, where loads turn out larger than estimated and steel a little weaker than it is said to be.

How much strength to hold in reserve is a choice the designer makes, and once it is made it fixes the stress a member may be allowed to carry. From that stress and the load, you can work out how thick a bar has to be, choose a size that is actually made, and then check that the bar will not stretch too far, which is the last step in turning a force into a member that can be ordered and built.

The smallest area for a given load is then the force divided by the allowable stress, and the bar chosen is the smallest stock size that is at least that large.

lessons.title: Shear force and bending moment

steps.headline: A cut through a beam shows what the material has to carry

lead.text: Take the beam of the opening, with its reactions of 21 kN and 14 kN, and imagine cutting it through 2 m from the left support. The left piece is now a body of its own, and like any body it must be in [[equilibrium|The state of a body at rest, in which the resultant of the forces on it is zero. Met in 'Forces as vectors'.]]. Only one force acts on it from outside, the 21 kN push of the support, and something has to balance it. The only thing left is the cut face, where the right half of the beam holds the left half, so the cut face must supply a downward force of 21 kN. The vertical force carried across a cut is called the **shear force**, V, because the two sides of the cut tend to slide past each other.

A second condition has to be met. The 21 kN reaction acts 2 m from the cut, so it tends to turn the left piece about the cut with a moment of 21 × 2 = 42 kN·m, and the cut face must supply an equal moment the other way. That moment is the **bending moment**, M, and it is what the material across the cut has to resist as the beam bends. A moment that makes the beam curve like a smile, with its bottom stretched and its top squeezed, is called **sagging**, and it is counted as positive.

afterFigure.text: At any cut, both are found from the forces on one side of it: V is the sum of the vertical forces on the left piece, with upward counted as positive, and M is the sum of their moments about the cut, with sagging positive. The right piece would give the same two answers, because the whole beam is in equilibrium.

steps.headline: Moving the cut along the beam draws the shear and moment diagrams

lead.text: Now slide the cut along the beam from A to B and record V and M at each position. Up to the load, 4 m from A, only the 21 kN reaction lies to its left, so V stays at +21 kN. As the cut passes the load, the 35 kN joins the left piece and pulls the total down, so V = 21 − 35 = −14 kN, and it stays there up to B. **A point load makes the shear jump down by its own size.**

The moment grows steadily while V is positive, since each metre of the cut adds another 21 kN × 1 m: it is 21 × 2 = 42 kN·m at 2 m and 21 × 4 = 84 kN·m at the load. Beyond the load the shear is negative, so the moment falls, to 21 × 6 − 35 × 2 = 56 kN·m at 6 m, and it reaches zero at B. The rate at which the moment changes along the beam is the *shear*: 21 kN·m for each metre on the left of the load and −14 kN·m for each metre on the right.

reveal.text: The bending moment is therefore greatest where the shear passes through zero, which is where it changes sign. For a point load that is under the load, and this is the quickest way to find the section a beam is designed for.

steps.headline: The moment peaks where the shear is zero, and spreading a load halves the peak

lead.text: A single load P at the midspan of a beam of length L is carried half by each support, so the moment under the load is (P ÷ 2) × (L ÷ 2), which is **PL ÷ 4**. Spreading the same load changes the picture, and the figure compares the two on a 6 m beam: 2 kN/m along its whole length, and the same 12 kN as one load at midspan. In both cases each support carries 6 kN.

With the single load the peak is 6 × 3 = 18 kN·m, which agrees with PL ÷ 4 = 12 × 6 ÷ 4. With the spread load the shear falls steadily from 6 kN at the left support to zero at midspan, which is where the moment peaks, and the left piece holds the 6 kN reaction at 3 m from the cut and 6 kN of load acting 1.5 m from it, so M = 6 × 3 − 6 × 1.5 = 9 kN·m. That agrees with **wL² ÷ 8**, which is 2 × 36 ÷ 8, where w is the load per metre and L is the span.

afterFigure.text: Spreading the load over the whole beam has halved the peak moment, because much of the load now sits near the supports, where it has little distance over which to turn the beam.

steps.headline: A cantilever has its largest moment at the wall

lead.text: A **cantilever** is a beam fixed at one end and free at the other, like a balcony or a diving board. With no support at the free end, the wall has to supply both a vertical force equal to the load and a moment. To find the shear and the moment at a cut, it is simplest to keep the piece away from the wall, because no reaction acts on it: the cut face has to balance the load on that piece.

In the first case of the figure, a 4 kN load hangs at the tip of a cantilever 5 m long. Every cut has the same shear, 4 kN, and the moment grows with the distance from the tip until it reaches 4 × 5 = 20 kN·m at the wall, where the beam is bent most. The beam curves with its top stretched, which is a **hogging** moment, the opposite of sagging, and the moment diagram is drawn negative. Spread the same 4 kN along the 5 m instead and, on average, it acts only 2.5 m from the wall, so the moment there halves to 4 × 2.5 = 10 kN·m.

reveal.text: Both pieces give the same moment, which is a check worth making: the right piece holds only the 24 kN reaction at B, 3 m from the cut, and 24 × 3 is again 72 kN·m.

lessons.orientation: Cut a beam and balance one piece to find the shear force and bending moment at any section, and where the moment peaks.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A beam 10 m long rests on a support at each end and carries a 35 kN load 4 m from the left end, so the supports push up with 21 kN on the left and 14 kN on the right. Those are the forces that act on the beam from outside. Inside it, every cross-section is doing a job of its own, since the material on one side of any cut has to hold up the material on the other side against the load, and has to resist the turning effect of forces that are not in line with the cut.

These internal demands change from place to place along the beam, and the place where the largest one occurs is the place the beam is designed for. They are found by cutting the beam and balancing one piece, which is nothing more than the equilibrium of the first three lessons applied to part of a beam.

intro.promise: By the end you'll cut a beam to find the shear force and bending moment at any section, and say where the moment is greatest.
intro.whyItMatters: A beam is designed for its largest bending moment, so the next lesson starts from it.

recap.keyIdea: At any cut the shear force is the sum of the vertical forces on one side and the bending moment is the sum of their moments about the cut, and the moment is greatest where the shear is zero.

blocks.text: A cut through a beam exposes the [[shear force|The vertical force carried across a cut through a beam. Met in 'A cut through a beam shows what the material has to carry'.]] and the [[bending moment|The moment carried across a cut through a beam, sagging positive. Met in 'A cut through a beam shows what the material has to carry'.]] that its two halves carry between them. The shear force is the sum of the vertical forces on one side of the cut, and the bending moment is the sum of their moments about the cut, and either side gives the same answers because the whole beam is in equilibrium.

The shear is the slope of the moment diagram, so **the bending moment is greatest where the shear is zero**. That gives PL ÷ 4 for a single load at midspan, wL² ÷ 8 for a load spread over the whole span, and the load times its distance, hogging, at the wall of a cantilever. The beam is designed for the section where the moment is greatest.

recap.nextHook: The material at that section is stretched on one side and squeezed on the other, and the next lesson turns the moment into the stress that it causes.

lessons.title: Bending stress and the I-beam

steps.headline: A bent beam is squeezed on one side and stretched on the other

lead.text: Bend a ruler between your hands and look along its edge. On the inside of the bend the material is squeezed, and on the outside it is stretched, and a loaded beam does the same. When it sags, its top surface becomes shorter and its bottom surface longer, and somewhere between them is a layer whose length does not change at all. That layer is the **neutral axis**, and in a symmetric section it runs through the middle of the depth. Galileo analysed the strength of a cantilever in his *Two New Sciences* of 1638, though he took the beam to turn about its lower edge and not about the neutral axis.

A layer twice as far from the neutral axis changes length twice as much, so its strain, and in the elastic range its stress, is twice as large. The layer farthest from the neutral axis, at the top or the bottom surface, is the **outer fibre**, and it carries the largest stress, compression above the neutral axis and tension below it for a sagging beam.

afterFigure.text: The stress is therefore not the same over the whole cross-section, as it was in a tie. It is zero on the neutral axis and rises in a straight line to its largest value at the outer fibre, which means that the material close to the neutral axis hardly works at all.

The second is the cross-section, with stress drawn as two triangles: compression above the neutral axis and tension below it.

reveal.text: Stress is zero on the neutral axis, so the material there does no work, and that is a hint about how a beam can be made lighter without making it much weaker.

steps.headline: Bending stress is the moment times the distance from the neutral axis, divided by I

lead.text: The [[bending moment|The moment carried across a cut through a beam, sagging positive. Met in 'Shear force and bending moment'.]] at a section is the total turning effect of the stresses across it, and a stress that grows in a straight line from zero at the neutral axis gives a simple result: at a distance y from the neutral axis the **bending stress** is **σ = M × y ÷ I**. The letter I stands for the **second moment of area** of the cross-section about its neutral axis, which measures how well the shape resists bending, and material far from the axis counts for much more than material close to it. For a solid rectangle of width b and depth h, **I = bh³ ÷ 12**, and its unit is mm⁴.

The units need care. A moment in kN·m is multiplied by 10⁶ to give N·mm, and then M in N·mm times y in mm, divided by I in mm⁴, gives a stress in N/mm², which is MPa. In the figure, the same 12,000 mm² of steel is bent by 4 kN·m in two ways. Wide and shallow, 120 mm wide and 100 mm deep, it has I = 120 × 100³ ÷ 12 = 10 × 10⁶ mm⁴, and its outer fibre, at y = 50 mm, carries 4 × 10⁶ × 50 ÷ (10 × 10⁶) = 20 MPa. Turned to be narrow and deep, 100 mm wide and 120 mm deep, I rises to 14.4 × 10⁶ mm⁴ and the outer fibre, now at 60 mm, carries only 16.7 MPa.

afterFigure.text: Both bars use exactly the same amount of steel. Standing the section on its deep side puts more of the material far from the neutral axis, and the stress falls by a sixth.

steps.headline: Finding the largest bending stress in a 150 mm by 250 mm beam under 30 kN·m

lead.text: A rectangular beam is 150 mm wide and 250 mm deep, and the bending moment at the section is 30 kN·m.

workedSteps.text: The neutral axis is at mid-depth, so the outer fibre is half the depth from it.
The second moment of area of a rectangle is bh³ ÷ 12.
Write the moment in N·mm, so that it agrees with mm and mm⁴.
The largest stress is at the outer fibre.

steps.headline: Finding the largest bending stress in a 100 mm by 200 mm beam under 20 kN·m

lead.text: The first two lines are set out, and the last one is yours.

workedSteps.text: The second moment of area of the rectangle is bh³ ÷ 12.
The outer fibre is half the depth from the neutral axis, and the moment is 20 × 10⁶ N·mm.
Use σ = M y ÷ I and give the stress in MPa.

steps.headline: Depth counts three times, so a deeper beam is far stiffer

lead.text: In I = bh³ ÷ 12 the width appears once and the depth appears *cubed*. A beam 50 mm wide and 100 mm deep has I = 50 × 100³ ÷ 12 = 4.17 × 10⁶ mm⁴, and made 50% deeper, at 150 mm, it has I = 14.06 × 10⁶ mm⁴, which is 1.5³, or 3.375 times as much, for 50% more material. A ruler shows the same thing: it bends easily when laid flat and hardly at all when it stands on its edge.

For a rectangle, the stress at the outer fibre also simplifies. Putting y = h ÷ 2 and I = bh³ ÷ 12 into σ = M y ÷ I gives **σ = 6M ÷ (bh²)**, so that for a given moment the largest stress falls with the *square* of the depth, and each millimetre of depth is worth more than a millimetre of width.

reveal.text: For the same width, doubling the depth makes the section eight times as stiff in I, and since the outer fibre is also twice as far out, the largest stress for a given moment falls to a quarter.

steps.headline: An I-beam puts its material where the stress is highest

lead.text: Material near the neutral axis carries little stress and adds little to I, so an efficient shape keeps most of its material at the top and bottom. An **I-section** does so: two wide **flanges** are joined by a thin **web**. Its second moment of area is that of the outer rectangle minus the two empty regions beside the web, **I = [B × H³ − (B − t) × h³] ÷ 12**, where B and H are the overall width and depth, t is the web thickness, and h is the clear depth between the flanges.

In the figure, an I-section 80 mm wide and 150 mm deep, with flanges 10 mm thick and a web 8 mm thick, is compared with a solid rectangle of the same outline. The I-section has an area of 2,640 mm², about a fifth of the rectangle's 12,000 mm², and yet its I is 9.3 × 10⁶ mm⁴ against 22.5 × 10⁶, which is about 41%. It keeps about 41% of the stiffness with 22% of the steel.

afterFigure.text: Under the same 10 kN·m the I-section's outer fibre is more highly stressed, at 80.5 MPa against 33.3 MPa, but the steel saved is large, which is why steel beams are rolled in this shape: the flanges carry the bending and the web mostly holds them apart.

lead.text: For a rectangle the largest bending stress is 6M ÷ (bh²), with M in N·mm.

reveal.text: Because the stress falls with the square of the depth, a modest increase in depth buys a large margin, and that is why deep, narrow sections are the economical choice when a beam can stand on edge.

lessons.orientation: Find the largest bending stress in a rectangular or I-shaped beam, and see why depth and flanges make a beam efficient.

blocks.text: A timber plank 50 mm thick and 200 mm wide, used as a floor joist, bends easily when it lies flat and hardly at all when it stands on its edge, although it is the same piece of timber with the same load and the same span. On edge it resists bending sixteen times as well, and the only thing that has changed is how far the wood lies from the middle of the plank's depth, about which it bends.

A steel beam goes further, since rolled into an I-shape, with its metal gathered into a wide strip at the top and another at the bottom, it carries the same bending as a solid bar with a fraction of the material. Both effects come from the way the stress in a bent beam is spread over its cross-section.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the largest bending stress in a rectangular or I-shaped beam, and see why depth and flanges matter.
intro.whyItMatters: The shape of a beam decides how much steel a given bending moment costs.

recap.keyIdea: The bending stress is σ = M × y ÷ I, zero at the neutral axis and largest at the outer fibre, and I grows with the cube of the depth.

blocks.text: In a bent beam the [[neutral axis|The layer of a bent beam whose length does not change, where the bending stress is zero. Met in 'A bent beam is squeezed on one side and stretched on the other'.]] is the layer that keeps its length, and the stress rises in a straight line from zero there to its largest value at the [[outer fibre|The layer of a beam farthest from the neutral axis, where the bending stress is largest. Met in 'A bent beam is squeezed on one side and stretched on the other'.]]: **σ = M × y ÷ I**, with M in N·mm, y in mm and I in mm⁴ giving MPa. I, the [[second moment of area|A property of a cross-section, I, that measures how well its shape resists bending, in mm⁴. Met in 'Bending stress is the moment times the distance from the neutral axis, divided by I'.]], is bh³ ÷ 12 for a rectangle, so it grows with the *cube* of the depth.

Depth is therefore the cheapest way to stiffen a beam, and the I-section carries the idea furthest: it puts its flanges at the outer fibres, where the stress is highest, and leaves little material near the neutral axis, where it would do almost nothing.

recap.nextHook: The same I decides how far a beam sags as well as how much it is stressed, and the next lesson turns it into a deflection.

lessons.title: Deflection and stiffness

steps.headline: A beam curves in proportion to its bending moment and in inverse proportion to EI

lead.text: Under load a beam bends into a curve, and the distance that a point on it moves from where it was is its **deflection**. For a cantilever, which is fixed at one end and free at the other, the deflection is greatest at the free tip. How sharply the beam curves at each point depends on two things: the [[bending moment|The moment carried across a cut through a beam, sagging positive. Met in 'Shear force and bending moment'.]] there, which tries to bend it, and the product of [[Young's modulus|The stress that goes with a strain of one in the elastic range, E, a property of the material. Met in 'Young's modulus ties stress to strain'.]] and the [[second moment of area|A property of a cross-section, I, that measures how well its shape resists bending, in mm⁴. Met in 'Bending stress and the I-beam'.]], **EI**, which resists. The product EI is called the **flexural rigidity**, and curvature = M ÷ EI.

Adding up the curvature along the whole length gives the deflection. Leonhard Euler worked this theory out in the 1740s, building on an idea of Daniel Bernoulli's. The two things to notice here are that the deflection grows when the moment grows and shrinks when EI grows.

steps.headline: A cantilever's tip deflection is PL³ ÷ 3EI

lead.text: Carrying out the addition for a cantilever of length L with a load P at its free end gives **δ = P L³ ÷ (3 E I)**. The symbols have to be in a consistent set of units, and the safe choice is base units: P in newtons, L in metres, E in pascals and I in m⁴, which gives δ in metres. For steel E = 200 GPa = 200 × 10⁹ Pa, and a section with I = 2 × 10⁶ mm⁴ has I = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴, because a millimetre to the fourth power is 10⁻¹² of a metre to the fourth. Then EI = 200 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁶ = 400,000 N·m².

In the figure, a 3 kN load on a steel cantilever 1 m long gives δ = 3,000 × 1³ ÷ (3 × 400,000) = 0.0025 m, or 2.5 mm, and the same load on a cantilever 3 m long gives 3,000 × 27 ÷ 1,200,000 = 0.0675 m, or 67.5 mm. The cantilever is three times as long and deflects 27 times as much, because the length appears *cubed*.

afterFigure.text: The formula shows how each quantity enters. The load P sits on top, so deflection is proportional to it, while E and I sit underneath, so a stiffer material or a bigger section reduces it, and the length is raised to the third power.

lead.text: The metal is aluminium this time, and the first two lines are set out.

Put the values into the tip formula.
Work it out in metres and give the deflection in mm.

steps.headline: Stiffness is load per unit of deflection, and each quantity scales in its own way

lead.text: The ratio of load to deflection, **k = P ÷ δ**, is the **stiffness** of the cantilever at its tip: the load needed for each unit of deflection. From the tip formula, **k = 3EI ÷ L³**. For the 1 m steel cantilever above it is 3 × 400,000 ÷ 1 = 1.2 × 10⁶ N/m, which is 1,200 kN/m, and for the 3 m one it is 27 times smaller, about 44 kN/m.

The formula also says how the deflection changes when one quantity changes and the others stay put. It is proportional to the load, so while the steel stays elastic, more load gives a proportionally larger deflection. It is inversely proportional to E and to I. And it is proportional to the *cube* of the length, which makes length by far the most powerful quantity: shortening a cantilever by a third cuts its deflection to less than a third of what it was.

reveal.text: Turned onto its side, so that it is 100 mm wide and 50 mm deep, the same bar would sag four times as far, 25.6 mm, because its I falls to a quarter. The way a bar is turned matters as much as its size.

lessons.orientation: Find the tip deflection of a cantilever from its load, length, material and section, and see how each quantity changes it.

blocks.text: A floor beam can be strong enough never to break and still be useless, because the floor bounces underfoot and the plaster cracks. A common limit for a floor beam is that it should sag by no more than about a 360th of its span, which is about 17 mm on a span of 6 m, and a beam that stays well inside its allowable stress can still sag far more than that.

How far a beam sags depends on the load, on its length, on its material and on the shape of its cross-section, and it does not depend on them all in the same way. The simplest case, a cantilever with a load at its tip, shows how each one enters, so that a beam can be chosen to limit its sag as well as to resist breaking.

intro.whyItMatters: A beam that is strong enough can still sag too far to be of use.

recap.keyIdea: A cantilever's tip deflection is PL³ ÷ 3EI, proportional to the load and the cube of the length and inversely proportional to EI.

blocks.text: The curvature of a beam is its bending moment divided by the [[flexural rigidity|The product EI, which measures how strongly a beam resists being curved. Met in 'A beam curves in proportion to its bending moment and in inverse proportion to EI'.]], EI, and adding the curvature along a cantilever gives the tip deflection **δ = PL³ ÷ 3EI**, worked in base units so that it comes out in metres. The tip stiffness, **k = P ÷ δ = 3EI ÷ L³**, is the load needed for each unit of deflection.

The deflection is proportional to the load, inversely proportional to E and to I, and proportional to the *cube* of the length, so a beam sized for strength is checked against its limit on sag, and shortening it is the most effective way of stiffening it.

recap.nextHook: From here the course turns from structures to machines, beginning with levers and pulleys, which trade force against distance on purpose.

lessons.title: Levers and pulleys

steps.headline: A lever trades force for distance in the ratio of its arms

lead.text: A **lever** is a rigid bar that turns about a fixed point called the **fulcrum**. A force applied to it, called the **effort**, moves or holds a load at another point of the bar. The distance from the fulcrum to the effort is the **effort arm**, and the distance from the fulcrum to the load is the **load arm**, each measured along the bar when the forces act at right angles to it.

When the lever is in balance, with a weightless bar and no friction, the [[moments|The turning effects of forces about a point: force times perpendicular distance. Met in 'Turning effect: moments'.]] about the fulcrum must be equal, **effort × effort arm = load × load arm**. Dividing, the load is the effort times the ratio of the arms, and that ratio, effort arm ÷ load arm, is the **mechanical advantage** of the lever. In the figure the effort arm is 1.0 m and the load arm 0.4 m, so a 450 N load is held by an effort of 450 × 0.4 ÷ 1.0 = 180 N, and the mechanical advantage is 1.0 ÷ 0.4 = 2.5. Lengthening the effort arm to 2.0 m raises the advantage to 5 and brings the effort down to 90 N.

afterFigure.text: The force has not come free. An effort arm 2.5 times the load arm means that the hand moves 2.5 times as far as the load, so if the load rises 0.1 m the effort moves 0.25 m, and the work in, 180 N × 0.25 m = 45 J, equals the work done on the load, 450 N × 0.1 m = 45 J. **A lever gives force in exchange for distance, and never gives energy.**

lead.text: A lever has an effort arm of 1.2 m and a load arm of 0.4 m, and it holds a load of 720 N in balance.

workedSteps.text: Balance the moments about the fulcrum, with the effort as the unknown.
Work out the moment of the load.
Divide by the effort arm.
As a check, the mechanical advantage is the ratio of the arms, and the effort is the load divided by it.

steps.headline: Finding the effort for a 900 N load with arms of 1.2 m and 0.2 m

lead.text: The first line sets the balance out and the last is yours.

workedSteps.text: Balance the moments about the fulcrum: the effort times its arm equals the load times its arm.
Solve for the effort and give it in N.

steps.headline: The position of the fulcrum gives three classes of lever

lead.text: The fulcrum, the effort and the load can be arranged along a bar in three ways. In a **first-class** lever the fulcrum is between the effort and the load, as in a crowbar or a see-saw. In a **second-class** lever the load is between the fulcrum and the effort, as in a wheelbarrow or a nutcracker. In a **third-class** lever the effort is between the fulcrum and the load, as in a pair of tweezers or a shovel.

The same balance of moments holds in all three, but the arms compare differently. In a second-class lever the effort arm is always the longer, so the mechanical advantage is above one and the effort is smaller than the load, as with the 840 N load held by 280 N in the figure. In a third-class lever the effort arm is always the shorter, so the advantage is *below* one and the effort has to be larger than the load, as with the 40 N load that takes 100 N of effort in the third case.

afterFigure.text: What a third-class lever gains is distance and speed: the load moves 2.5 times as far as the effort does, which is what makes tweezers, fishing rods and the human forearm useful.

reveal.text: The class is set by what is in the middle: the fulcrum for first class, the load for second class, the effort for third class. A second-class lever always multiplies force, and a third-class lever always multiplies distance.

lead.text: The forearm is a third-class lever.

steps.headline: A pulley system shares the load between its strands and pays in rope

lead.text: A rope passed round pulleys can lift a load with less force than the load itself. The moving block that carries the load hangs from several lengths of rope, called **strands**, and in an ideal system, with no friction and weightless pulleys, the same tension acts all along the rope. Each of the n supporting strands therefore carries an equal share, so **the [[effort|The force applied to a machine to move or hold its load. Met in 'A lever trades force for distance in the ratio of its arms'.]], the pull on the free end, is the load divided by n**, and the mechanical advantage is n.

The price is rope. To lift the load by a height h, every one of the supporting strands has to shorten by h, so the free end must be pulled through n × h of rope. In the figure, a system with 2 supporting strands lifts 720 N with an effort of 360 N, and to raise the load 0.5 m the hand pulls 1 m of rope. With 6 strands the effort falls to 120 N, and the hand pulls 3 m of rope for the same 0.5 m lift.

afterFigure.text: In both cases the effort times the rope pulled is 360 J, equal to the load times the lift, 720 N × 0.5 m. It is the same exchange as in the lever: the force is divided by the number of strands, and the distance is multiplied by it.

reveal.text: The answer is the load times the lift, 960 × 0.75, so the pulley system gives out exactly the work that was put into it. In a real system friction takes a share of that work, which a later lesson counts.

lessons.orientation: Trade force for distance with levers and rope systems, and count what each one costs.

blocks.text: A person pushing with 300 N on the end of a bar 1.0 m long can raise a 1,500 N block of stone that rests on it 0.2 m from the pivot. The block weighs five times the push, and the bar has not made force from nothing: the hand moves five times as far as the block does. Every simple machine, from a crowbar to a block and tackle, works in the same way, giving force in exchange for distance.

Because a machine gives nothing for free, the force a lever or a block and tackle needs can be worked out from its shape alone, before it is built, and the same accounting tells you how far the hand or the rope has to travel to raise the load by a given height.

recap.keyIdea: A machine trades force for distance, so the force gained is the distance paid: a lever by the ratio of its arms and a pulley system by the number of its supporting strands.

blocks.text: A lever in balance has equal [[moments|The turning effects of forces about a point: force times perpendicular distance. Met in 'Turning effect: moments'.]] on its two sides, so **effort × effort arm = load × load arm**, and its [[mechanical advantage|The load divided by the effort. For a lever, the effort arm divided by the load arm. Met in 'A lever trades force for distance in the ratio of its arms'.]] is the ratio of the arms. The position of the fulcrum gives three classes: a first-class lever has the fulcrum in the middle, a second-class one the load, which always multiplies force, and a third-class one the effort, which multiplies distance and speed.

In an ideal pulley system the [[strands|The lengths of rope that support a pulley system's moving block. Met in 'A pulley system shares the load between its strands and pays in rope'.]] that support the block share the load, so the effort is the load divided by their number, and the rope pulled through is their number times the lift. In every one of these machines the work put in equals the work done, the force gained being the distance given up.
