lessons.title: Gear trains: speed and torque

steps.headline: Meshing gears turn at speeds in inverse proportion to their teeth

lead.text: A **gear** is a wheel with teeth, and two gears whose teeth fit together are said to **mesh**. The gear that is turned by the motor or the pedals is the **driver**, and the gear it turns is the **driven** gear. At the point where the teeth meet, the two rims move at the same speed, so every tooth of the driver that passes the mesh pushes one tooth of the driven gear past it, and **the number of teeth passing the mesh each minute is the same for both gears**.

That gives the speed of the driven gear as the driver's speed multiplied by driver teeth ÷ driven teeth, with speeds in revolutions per minute, written rpm. In the figure, a 20-tooth driver turning at 600 rpm drives a 40-tooth gear at 600 × 20 ÷ 40 = 300 rpm: the driven gear has twice the teeth, so it turns at half the speed. The ratio of driven teeth to driver teeth, 2 here, is the **gear ratio**, and a ratio above one, which slows the output, is called a *reduction*.

afterFigure.text: The first case, two gears of 20 teeth each, has a ratio of 1, so the output turns at the same speed, but in the opposite direction, which is the other thing that a mesh does and which the later screens use.

steps.headline: A gear pair trades speed for torque, and the product stays the same

lead.text: A gear pair changes the [[torque|The moment of a force about an axis or shaft, in N·m. Met in 'Turning effect: moments'.]] on a shaft as well as its speed. If the mesh wastes nothing, the power that passes from one shaft to the other is unchanged, and the power of a turning shaft is its torque times its speed, so **torque times speed is the same on the output shaft as on the input**. A pair that cuts the speed to a half must therefore double the torque.

Take the 20-tooth driver and the 40-tooth gear of the last screen, with 10 N·m on the input shaft at 600 rpm. The output turns at 300 rpm, half the speed, so its torque is twice as large, 20 N·m, and the product of torque and speed is 6,000 on both shafts. In general **the output torque is the input torque multiplied by the gear ratio**, and the output speed is the input speed divided by it. A real mesh loses a little to friction, which the last lesson counts. Here the mesh is taken as lossless.

steps.headline: Finding the speed and torque after a 25-tooth driver meshes with a 100-tooth gear

lead.text: A 25-tooth driver turns at 1,200 rpm and carries 8 N·m. It meshes with a 100-tooth gear, and the mesh is lossless.

workedSteps.text: The gear ratio is the driven teeth divided by the driver teeth.
The output speed is the input speed divided by the ratio.
The output torque is the input torque multiplied by the ratio.
As a check, the product of torque and speed must be the same on both shafts.

steps.headline: An idler changes the direction of the output but not the ratio

lead.text: Each mesh between two gears reverses the direction of rotation, so a driver and a driven gear in direct mesh turn in opposite directions. Place a third gear between them, called an **idler**, and there are two meshes, so the output turns the same way as the driver again. In the figure, a 24-tooth driver turning at 600 rpm drives a 48-tooth gear at 300 rpm, whether through a 36-tooth idler or by direct mesh, and only the direction differs.

The idler's teeth do not affect the output speed, because the idler is driven by the first gear at its rim speed and passes the same rim speed on to the second. It does turn at a speed of its own, found from the mesh rule: 600 × 24 ÷ 36 = 400 rpm. **The output depends only on the driver and the driven gear, and the idler's teeth cancel out.** Idlers are used to keep the direction the same, or to bridge a gap between shafts that is wider than the two gears.

reveal.text: An even number of meshes returns the direction to the driver's, and an odd number reverses it. The idler adds one mesh and so flips the direction once more.

steps.headline: Gear pairs on a shared shaft multiply their ratios, and a chain acts like a mesh

lead.text: To get a large reduction, two pairs of gears can be placed one after the other, with the driven gear of the first pair on the same shaft as the driver of the second. This is a **compound train**, and **the overall ratio is the product of the ratios of the pairs**. In the figure, a 12-tooth gear drives a 36-tooth one, a ratio of 3, and on the same shaft as the 36-tooth gear a 10-tooth gear drives a 50-tooth one, a ratio of 5. The overall ratio is 3 × 5 = 15, so an input of 1,500 rpm and 4 N·m becomes 100 rpm and 60 N·m.

A chain drive follows the same rule. A chain joins two toothed wheels, so the same number of teeth pass each wheel every minute, and the ratio is again driven teeth ÷ driver teeth, but because the chain wraps both wheels they turn in the *same* direction. On the bicycle of the opening, with 44 teeth at the pedals and 22 on the back wheel, the wheel turns twice for every turn of the pedals. John Kemp Starley's Rover safety bicycle of 1885 put the chain drive on the rear wheel, and set the pattern of the modern bicycle.

reveal.text: The output turns at 300 rpm, one eighth of the input speed, and both pairs are external meshes, so the output turns the same way as the input. The torque has gone up by exactly the factor by which the speed has fallen.

lessons.orientation: Find the speed, torque and direction at the output of a gear train, an idler or a chain from the tooth counts.

blocks.text: A bicycle's chainring at the pedals has 44 teeth and the sprocket on its back wheel has 22, and since the chain carries the same number of teeth past each of them, the back wheel turns twice for every turn of the pedals, at 120 rpm when the rider pedals at 60 rpm. On a hill the rider shifts to a sprocket of 33 teeth, which slows the back wheel to 80 rpm, so that each push on the pedals counts for more at the road.

Every geared machine, from a clock to the gearbox of a wind turbine, makes the same trade between speed and turning force, and the number of teeth on each wheel decides it. From the tooth counts of a train of gears you can work out how fast its output turns, how much turning force it delivers and which way it goes.

intro.whyItMatters: Gears and chains match a fast motor to a slow, heavy load.

recap.keyIdea: Meshing gears pass the same number of teeth each minute, so the output speed is the input speed divided by the gear ratio, and for a lossless mesh the torque is multiplied by it.

blocks.text: Meshing gears pass the same number of teeth each minute, so the driven gear turns at the driver's speed divided by the [[gear ratio|The driven gear's teeth divided by the driver's teeth. Met in 'Meshing gears turn at speeds in inverse proportion to their teeth'.]], driven teeth ÷ driver teeth, and for a lossless mesh **the torque is multiplied by that ratio**, since torque times speed is unchanged. A ratio above one is a reduction: slower, with more torque.

An [[idler|A gear placed between a driver and a driven gear, which reverses the direction and drops out of the ratio. Met in 'An idler changes the direction of the output but not the ratio'.]] reverses the direction once more and drops out of the ratio, a [[compound train|Gear pairs placed one after another on shared shafts, so that their ratios multiply. Met in 'Gear pairs on a shared shaft multiply their ratios, and a chain acts like a mesh'.]] multiplies the ratios of its pairs, and a chain behaves as a mesh that keeps the direction. In all of them the output depends on the tooth counts and not on the sizes of the shafts.

lessons.title: Efficiency and power in a drive

steps.headline: Power is the rate of doing work, and for a moving force it is force times speed

lead.text: Work is a force acting through a distance, but a machine is also judged by how quickly it works, and the rate of doing work is called **power**. Its unit is the **watt**, W, which is one joule each second. The unit is named for James Watt, whose improved steam engines were sold by comparison with the horses they replaced, and who rated them in horsepower, a unit now taken as about 746 W.

When a force F moves its point of application at a speed v, in the direction of the force, it does F × v of work each second, so **power = force × speed**. In the figure, a hoist lifts a 400 N load. At 0.5 m/s it raises 400 N through 0.5 m each second, which is 200 J every second, or 200 W, and at 1.5 m/s the same load takes 600 W. The load has not changed and the speed has tripled, so the power is three times as large.

steps.headline: For a turning shaft, power is torque times angular speed in radians per second

lead.text: A shaft does not move a force along a line, it turns, but the same idea holds: the work done by a [[torque|The moment of a force about an axis or shaft, in N·m. Met in 'Turning effect: moments'.]] T in turning through an angle θ, in radians, is T × θ, so the power is **P = T × ω**, where ω (omega) is the **angular speed**, in radians per second. The units need care, because shaft speeds are quoted in rpm. One revolution is 2π radians and a minute is 60 seconds, so **ω = N × 2π ÷ 60**, with N in rpm.

In the figure, a motor delivers 8 N·m at 300 rpm. The angular speed is 300 × 2π ÷ 60 = 31.42 rad/s, so the power is 8 × 31.42 = 251 W. At 600 rpm the angular speed doubles to 62.83 rad/s, and so does the power, to 503 W. Putting the rpm straight into the formula would give a number that is not in watts at all, and the conversion to radians per second is what makes the result a power.

steps.headline: Finding the power of a motor that delivers 25 N·m at 960 rpm

lead.text: A motor shaft carries 25 N·m and turns at 960 rpm. The power is the torque times the angular speed.

workedSteps.text: Convert the speed to radians per second.
Multiply the torque by the angular speed.
As a check, 25 N·m at about 100 rad/s is about 2,500 W, so the result is of the right size.

steps.headline: Each stage passes on only part of the power, and the efficiencies multiply

lead.text: No machine passes on all the power it receives. Friction between teeth, in bearings and in the lubricant turns part of it into heat, and the fraction that is passed on is the **efficiency**, written η (eta): **η = output power ÷ input power**. A well-made gear mesh may pass on 95% or more, but the loss is never zero, and it is counted stage by stage.

In the figure, each mesh is 90% efficient and the input is 4 N·m at 1,200 rpm, which is 503 W. One stage with a ratio of 3 passes on 0.9 of it, 452 W, and its output torque is 4 × 3 × 0.9 = 10.8 N·m, which is 90% of the ideal 12 N·m. Two stages in a row, with a combined ratio of 15, pass on 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81 of the power, 407 W, and the output torque is 4 × 15 × 0.81 = 48.6 N·m. **The efficiencies of stages in series multiply**, so every added stage costs more.

afterFigure.text: In general the output torque is the input torque times the [[gear ratio|The driven gear's teeth divided by the driver's teeth. Met in 'Gear trains: speed and torque'.]] times the efficiency: the ratio multiplies the torque, and the efficiency scales it down, while the output power is the input power times the efficiency.

steps.headline: A motor must supply more power than the load receives

lead.text: The useful power of a hoist is the load times the speed at which it is lifted, but the motor has to supply more than that, because the efficiency of the drive takes its share first: **motor power = useful power ÷ efficiency**. In the figure, a hoist with 3 supporting strands lifts 1,800 N at 0.4 m/s. The useful power is 1,800 × 0.4 = 720 W, and if the pulleys are 75% efficient the motor must supply 720 ÷ 0.75 = 960 W, the 240 W difference being lost as heat.

Friction also raises the effort. An ideal system with n strands divides the load by n, but with an efficiency η the effort is the load ÷ (n × η), so the actual [[mechanical advantage|The load divided by the effort. For a lever, the effort arm divided by the load arm. Met in 'Levers and pulleys'.]] is only n × η. Here the effort is 1,800 ÷ (3 × 0.75) = 800 N instead of the ideal 600 N, while the rope pulled through is still n times the lift.

reveal.text: Gearing never gives something for nothing. Each reduction trades output speed for torque, and each added stage wastes a little more of the power that the motor supplies.
The hook receives 942.5 W of the 1,256.6 W that the motor delivers, and at 0.6 m/s that supports a force of 1,571 N, which is a mass of about 160 kg.

lessons.orientation: Follow power from a hoist's load back to its motor through each stage, counting the losses, and find the power, torque and motor size.

blocks.text: A small hoist lifts a 1,200 N load at 0.5 m/s, which delivers 600 W at the hook, yet the motor fitted to it is rated at 800 W. The extra 200 W is the share of the power that the gears and pulleys turn into heat before it reaches the load, so a 600 W motor could not lift that load at that speed at all, however its drive was geared.

Each stage of a drive trades speed for force or torque and loses part of the power it passes on, so following the power from the load back to the motor, stage by stage, tells you how large a motor a machine needs and how much it can lift with the motor it has.

intro.whyItMatters: A motor chosen without the losses is too small for its load.

recap.keyIdea: Power is force times speed, or torque times angular speed, and the efficiencies of the stages multiply, so the motor has to supply the useful power divided by the overall efficiency.

blocks.text: The [[power|The rate of doing work: force times speed, in watts. Met in 'Power is the rate of doing work, and for a moving force it is force times speed'.]] of a moving load is **force × speed**, and the power of a shaft is **torque × angular speed**, with ω = 2π × rpm ÷ 60 in radians per second so that the result comes out in watts. The [[efficiency|The output power divided by the input power. Met in 'Each stage passes on only part of the power, and the efficiencies multiply'.]] of a stage is its output power divided by its input power, and **the efficiencies of stages in series multiply**.

Losses lower the output torque by the efficiency, raise the effort of a pulley system to load ÷ (n × η), and raise the power that the motor must supply to the useful power divided by the efficiency. A drive that gains torque pays for it in *speed*, and in a little more loss with every added stage.

questions.prompt: A 10 kN force acts at 30° above the horizontal. Find its horizontal component, in kN, to two decimal places.
hints: The horizontal side of the triangle is the one that touches the 30° angle.
The side that touches the angle takes the cosine, so the share is F cos θ.
Calculate 10 × cos 30° and round to two decimal places.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Horizontal component = 10 cos 30° = 8.660 kN, which rounds to 8.66 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 8.66 kN: the side touching the angle takes the cosine, so the horizontal part is F cos θ.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 10 sin 30°, the vertical part. The horizontal side touches the angle, so it takes the cosine.
That is the whole force. A slanted force has only part of itself acting across.

questions.prompt: Vertical component (kN)
hints: Which side of the slope triangle is the rise?
The vertical share is rise over long side.
Multiply the pull by that share.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The slope triangle 3–4–5 gives sin θ = 3/5, so the vertical component is 5 × 3/5 = 3 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 3 kN: the pull times rise over long side. Any slope triangle gives the shares without a calculator.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the horizontal part: the run over the long side. The vertical part uses the rise.
That is the whole pull. Only a fraction of it acts upward.
The share is over the long side of the triangle, not over the run.

questions.prompt: A pin carries 3 kN acting horizontally and 4 kN acting vertically. Find the size of their resultant, in kN.
hints: The two forces are at right angles, so their sizes do not simply add.
The resultant is the long side of the right-angled triangle formed by the two forces.
Use Pythagoras on the two sizes.
questions.onCorrect: 5 kN: square the two forces, add, and take the root, which gives the long side of the force triangle.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sizes, which works only for forces on one line. These two are at right angles.
That is the sum of the squares. The last step is to take the square root, which turns it back into a force.

questions.prompt: A ring is held by a force of 6 kN along +x and a force of 8 kN along +y. What size, in kN, must a third force have to keep the ring in equilibrium?
hints: In equilibrium the three forces have a resultant of zero.
The third force must be equal and opposite to the resultant of the other two.
The 6 kN and 8 kN forces are at right angles, so combine them with Pythagoras.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The third force must cancel the resultant of the first two: √(6² + 8²) = 10 kN, pointing opposite it.

questions.onCorrect: 10 kN, pointing opposite to the resultant of the other two forces: a closed set of forces means equilibrium.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two sizes. The forces are at right angles, so find their resultant first.
That is the difference of the sizes. The forces are at right angles, not opposed.

questions.prompt: Forces of 12 kN along +x and 5 kN along +y act on the pin of a gusset plate. Find the size of their resultant in kN.
hints: The 12 kN and 5 kN forces are at right angles to one another.
Square each force, add the squares, then take the square root.
Calculate √(144 + 25).
questions.onCorrect: 13 kN: at right angles, square, add and take the root.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sizes. Forces at right angles combine by Pythagoras.
That is the sum of the squares. The last step is the square root.

questions.prompt: A lamp hangs from two cables. Its free-body diagram isolates the lamp. Which force belongs on that diagram?
hints: The diagram is of the lamp alone, so ask which forces act on the lamp.
A force belongs on the diagram only if something pushes or pulls the lamp.
Check each option for what the force acts on.

acceptedIdeas: The pull of each cable on the lamp
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The pull of each cable on the lamp. The cable pulls act on the lamp, so they belong on its diagram.

choices.label: The pull of the lamp on the ceiling
The weight of the ceiling
The pull of each cable on the lamp

questions.onCorrect: The lamp's diagram holds its weight and the pull of each cable, because those are the forces that act on the lamp.

misconceptions.feedback: That force acts on the ceiling, not on the lamp, so it belongs on the ceiling's diagram.
The ceiling's weight acts on the ceiling. It does not act on the lamp.

questions.prompt: A 150 N force pushes at right angles to a spanner, 0.3 m from the bolt. Find the moment about the bolt, in N·m.
hints: The push is at right angles to the spanner, so the distance along the spanner is the perpendicular distance.
A moment is the force times that distance.
Multiply 150 N by 0.3 m.
questions.onCorrect: 45 N·m: force times perpendicular distance.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the force alone. A moment multiplies it by the distance as well.
That divides the force by the distance. A moment multiplies them.

questions.prompt: A 150 N force acts at 30° to a spanner's handle, at a point 0.3 m from the bolt. Find the size of its moment about the bolt, in N·m.
hints: Only the part of the force across the handle turns the spanner.
The across part is the force times the sine of the angle to the handle.
Multiply 150 × sin 30° by 0.3 m.
questions.onCorrect: 22.5 N·m: the across part is 150 sin 30°, which is half the force.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the moment of a push at right angles to the handle. At 30° only part of the push turns the spanner.
That uses cos 30°, the part along the handle, which has no turning effect.

questions.prompt: A 200 N force pulls along a spanner's handle, directly away from the bolt, at a point 0.3 m from it. What moment does it have about the bolt?
hints: Draw the line of action of the force, extended in both directions.
Where does that line pass in relation to the bolt?
The moment is the force times the perpendicular distance from the bolt to the line of action.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No moment at all: the line of action passes through the bolt, so the perpendicular distance and the moment are both zero.

choices.label: Some moment, but less than 60 N·m
60 N·m, the force times its distance from the bolt
No moment at all

questions.onCorrect: Zero: the line of action runs straight through the pivot, so the perpendicular distance is nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the force by the distance along the handle. A moment uses the distance at right angles to the line of action, and this line runs straight through the bolt.
A pull at a slight slant would give a moment smaller than 60 N·m, but this pull lies exactly along the handle, so its line of action passes through the bolt and the perpendicular distance is zero.

questions.prompt: A 300 N child sits 2 m to the left of a see-saw's pivot. How far to the right of the pivot, in metres, must a 400 N child sit for the see-saw to balance?
hints: The see-saw balances when the anticlockwise moment equals the clockwise moment.
The left child's moment is 300 × 2. The right child's is 400 times the unknown distance.
Set the two equal and divide by 400.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Balance needs 400 × d = 300 × 2 = 600 N·m, so d = 1.5 m.

misconceptions.feedback: Equal distances balance only equal weights. The heavier child must sit nearer the pivot.
That divides by the wrong weight. The left child's moment, 600 N·m, is divided by the right child's weight.

questions.prompt: A door handle is 0.8 m from the hinges. It is pulled with 40 N at right angles to the door. Find the moment about the hinges, in N·m.
hints: The hinges are the pivot, and the pull is at right angles to the door.
At right angles, the moment is the force multiplied by its distance from the pivot.
Multiply 40 N by 0.8 m.
questions.onCorrect: 32 N·m: force times distance, since the pull is at right angles to the door.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the force and the distance, which are different kinds of quantity. A moment multiplies them.
That divides the force by the distance. A moment multiplies them.

questions.prompt: To loosen a tight nut with the least effort, where and how should you push on the spanner?
hints: The moment is the across-part of the push times its distance from the nut.
Which position gives the longest distance from the nut?
Which direction gives the whole push as an across-part?

acceptedIdeas: At the end of the handle, at right angles to it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At the end of the handle, at right angles to it. The largest perpendicular distance gives the largest moment, and only a push at right angles uses all of it.

Near the nut, at right angles to the handle
At the end of the handle, along its length

questions.onCorrect: The end of the handle gives the longest arm, and a push at right angles puts all of the force across it.

questions.prompt: A 6 m beam rests on a pin at A and a roller at B, 6 m apart. It carries 12 kN at 2 m from A. Take moments about A to find the reaction at B, in kN.
hints: About A, the load turns the beam clockwise and RB turns it anticlockwise.
The two moments are equal: 6 × RB = 12 × 2.
Divide 24 by 6.
questions.onCorrect: 4 kN: 6RB = 12 × 2, so the support farther from the load carries the smaller share.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the moment of the load about A, in kN·m. Divide it by the 6 m between the supports to get a force.
That is the reaction at A, the support nearer the load. Moments about A give the other one.

questions.prompt: Reaction at A (kN)
hints: The two reactions together carry the whole load.
What is the load, and how much does B take?
Calculate 12 − 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: RA = 12 − RB = 12 − 4 = 8 kN. Moments about B confirm it: 12 × 4 ÷ 6 = 8 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 8 kN. A is nearer the load, so it carries more: the reactions add up to the load.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the reaction at B. A is nearer the load, so it carries more.
That would be the share if the load sat at the middle. This load is nearer A.

questions.prompt: A 6 m beam rests on supports at its two ends and carries 4 kN/m over its first 3 m. Find the reaction at the right-hand support, in kN.
hints: Replace the spread load by a single force and find where it acts.
The force is the load per metre times the loaded length, and it acts at the middle of the loaded length.
Take moments about the left support: 6R = (force) × (distance of the force from the left support).

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The spread load totals 4 × 3 = 12 kN acting at x = 1.5 m. About the left support: 6R = 12 × 1.5, so R = 3 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 3 kN: the spread load is 12 kN acting 1.5 m from the left support, so 6R = 12 × 1.5.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total of the spread load. Its moment about the left support uses its distance, 1.5 m, from the middle of the loaded length.
That is the left reaction. The question asks for the right-hand support.
That shares the load equally, but the load sits only on the left half of the beam.

questions.prompt: A beam rests on supports at 0 and at 4 m, and carries a 10 kN load at its free end, 6 m from the left support. Taking upward as positive, find the reaction at the support at 0, in kN.
hints: Take moments about the support at 0 to find the reaction at 4 m first.
Solve 4 × R = 10 × 6, then subtract from the load.
The vertical forces add to zero: RA + RB = 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: About x = 0: 4RB = 10 × 6, so RB = 15 kN. Then RA = 10 − 15 = −5 kN: the left support pulls down.

questions.onCorrect: −5 kN: the support at 4 m carries 15 kN, so the one at 0 pulls the beam down by 5 kN.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign. With upward positive, a support that holds the beam down has a negative reaction.
That is the reaction at the other support. Subtract it from the load to get this one.

questions.prompt: A 10 m beam rests on supports at its two ends. It carries 20 kN at 3 m from the left end and 10 kN at 8 m from the left end. Find the left reaction, in kN.
hints: Take moments about the right-hand support, so that only the left reaction remains unknown.
The loads are 7 m and 2 m from the right-hand support.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: About the right support: 10RA = 20 × 7 + 10 × 2 = 160, so RA = 16 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 16 kN: 10RA = 140 + 20 = 160, taking moments about the right-hand support.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the reaction at the other support. The question asks for the left one.
That is the sum of the moments, in kN·m. Divide by the 10 m span to get a force.

questions.prompt: Name the support that stops a beam moving vertically but lets it slide horizontally and turn.
hints: The support is described by the movements it allows: sliding and turning.
One kind of support holds the beam against sliding as well as against moving vertically.
The support is named for the way it lets the beam roll along it.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A roller support: it pushes at right angles to its surface and nothing more.

questions.onCorrect: A roller allows sliding and turning, and resists only movement up or down.

misconceptions.feedback: A pin also stops the beam sliding. The support described lets it slide.
A fixed support stops the beam turning as well. This one lets it turn.

questions.prompt: A triangular truss spans 4 m, with its apex C 1.5 m above the supports, so each sloping member is 2.5 m long. A 12 kN load hangs at C. Find the force in the sloping member AC, in kN.
hints: Isolate joint C, where the two sloping members and the load meet.
Each sloping member's vertical part is its force times 1.5/2.5, and the two parts together carry the load.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At C, both sloping members have vertical parts of F × 1.5/2.5. Then 2 × 0.6F = 12, so F = 10 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 10 kN, in compression: the two members each give a vertical part of 0.6F, and 1.2F = 12.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the second sloping member. Both members share the load at the apex.
That is each member's vertical part. The member itself carries more, because it slants.

questions.prompt: A triangular truss carries a load at its apex, and its two sloping members push outward on the feet. Is the bottom member AB, which joins the feet, in tension or compression?
hints: At a foot, the sloping member pushes outward, tending to spread the feet apart.
The bottom member has to stop the feet spreading, so think about which way it acts on them.
A member that holds two joints together pulls on them.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Tension: AB pulls inward to stop the supports spreading apart.

questions.onCorrect: The bottom member holds the feet together, so it pulls on its joints and is in tension.

misconceptions.feedback: A member in compression pushes on its joints. AB has to stop the feet spreading, so it pulls them together.

questions.prompt: In that truss, which spans 4 m with its apex 1.5 m up so that each sloping member is 2.5 m long, each sloping member carries 10 kN in compression. Find the force in the bottom member AB, in kN.
hints: Isolate joint A. The sloping member pushes on it down and outward.
The bottom member must balance the horizontal part of that push.
The horizontal part is the force times run over length: 10 × 2/2.5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Horizontal balance at A: FAB = 10 × 2/2.5 = 8 kN, in tension.

questions.onCorrect: 8 kN, in tension: the bottom member balances the horizontal part of the 10 kN push.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the force in the sloping member, along the slope. The bottom member balances only its horizontal part.
That is the vertical part, which the support's reaction balances. The bottom member balances the horizontal part.

questions.prompt: A king-post truss adds a vertical member DC from the middle of the bottom chord, D, up to the apex C. The only load is 12 kN at C. Find the force in DC, in kN.
hints: Isolate joint D, where AD, DB and DC meet, and note that no load acts there.
AD and DB lie along one horizontal line, so they have no vertical parts.
Balance the vertical forces at D.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At D, AD and DB are collinear and horizontal and no load acts, so vertical balance leaves DC with no force.

questions.onCorrect: Zero: at D, the two horizontal members have no vertical part and nothing hangs there, so DC has nothing to balance.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the load, but it acts at C and not at D. At joint D there is no load for DC to carry.

questions.prompt: A triangular truss spans 3 m, with its apex 2 m above the supports, so each sloping member is 2.5 m long. A 16 kN load acts at the apex. Find the tension in the bottom member, in kN.
hints: Find the force in the sloping members first, from the vertical balance at the apex.
At a foot, the bottom member balances the horizontal part of a sloping member.
The horizontal part is the force times 1.5/2.5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At the apex: 2F × 2/2.5 = 16, so F = 10 kN in each sloping member. At a support: tension = 10 × 1.5/2.5 = 6 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 6 kN: each sloping member carries 10 kN, and 1.5/2.5 of that acts along the bottom.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the force in each sloping member. The bottom member balances only its horizontal part.
That is the vertical part of a sloping member. The bottom member balances the horizontal part.

questions.prompt: A member pushes outward on the joints at both its ends. Is it in tension or compression?
hints: A member in tension pulls on its joints.
Think about whether this member is being stretched or squeezed.
A member that pushes on its joints is being shortened.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Compression: a strut pushes on its joints.

questions.onCorrect: A member that pushes on its joints is squeezed, which is compression.

misconceptions.feedback: A member in tension pulls on its joints, towards each other. This one pushes them apart.

questions.prompt: A steel bar with a cross-section of 400 mm² carries an axial pull of 20 kN. Find the stress in the bar, in MPa.
hints: Stress is force divided by cross-sectional area.
Convert 20 kN to newtons, since the area is in mm².
Divide 20,000 N by 400 mm².
questions.onCorrect: 50 MPa: 20,000 N over 400 mm².

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves the force in kilonewtons, so it is a thousand times too small. Convert to newtons first.
That is the force in newtons. Divide it by the area.

questions.prompt: A steel rod (E = 200 GPa) 2 m long works at a stress of 50 MPa. Find its stretch, in mm.
hints: The strain is the stress divided by E, with E in MPa.
The stretch is the strain times the original length, with the length in mm.
Multiply 0.00025 by 2,000.
questions.onCorrect: 0.5 mm: a strain of 0.00025 acting over 2,000 mm.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the strain, a ratio. Multiply it by the length to get a stretch.
Check E: 200 GPa is 200,000 MPa, a thousand times more than 200.

questions.prompt: An aluminium bar (E = 70 GPa) 1,400 mm long carries a stress of 50 MPa. Find its stretch, in mm.
hints: The strain is the stress divided by E, with E in MPa.
70 GPa is 70,000 MPa.
The stretch is the strain times 1,400 mm.
questions.onCorrect: 1 mm: a strain of 50/70,000 acting over 1,400 mm.

misconceptions.feedback: E has to be in MPa to match the stress. 70 GPa is 70,000 MPa.
That is the stretch of the steel bar of the previous question, which was longer. Aluminium is less stiff, and this bar is shorter.

questions.prompt: A steel bar with a yield stress of 250 MPa and an ultimate strength of 400 MPa is loaded to 300 MPa and then unloaded. What happens to it?
hints: Compare the 300 MPa with the yield stress.
Above the yield stress, is the stretch still fully recoverable?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It keeps a permanent stretch. 300 MPa is past yield but below the ultimate strength, so the bar survives with a permanent set.

choices.label: It keeps a permanent stretch
It has already fractured
It returns to its original length

questions.onCorrect: The stress went above the yield stress, so part of the stretch is permanent when the load is removed.

misconceptions.feedback: A bar springs back fully only below its yield stress. This load is above it.
Fracture needs the ultimate strength, 400 MPa. This load is below it.

questions.prompt: A square steel rod 10 mm × 10 mm carries an axial pull of 15 kN. Find the stress in the rod, in MPa.
hints: Stress is the force divided by the cross-sectional area, with the force in newtons.
The cross-section is a square, so its area is the side times the side.
Divide 15,000 N by the area in mm².
questions.onCorrect: 150 MPa: 15,000 N spread over 100 mm².

misconceptions.feedback: That is the force in newtons. Divide it by the area to get the force on each square millimetre.
That divides by the side, 10 mm, and not by the area. Multiply the two sides to get the area first.

questions.prompt: A steel tie (E = 200 GPa) 5 m long works at a stress of 100 MPa. Find its stretch, in mm.
hints: The strain is the stress divided by E, with E in MPa.
The stretch is the strain times the length, and the answer is wanted in mm.
Convert the 5 m to millimetres before multiplying.
questions.onCorrect: 2.5 mm: a strain of 100/200,000 over 5,000 mm.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves the length in metres. The answer is wanted in millimetres.
Check E: use 200,000 MPa, and not 200.

questions.prompt: A steel tie with a yield stress of 250 MPa has a cross-section of 400 mm² and carries 40 kN. Find its factor of safety against yield.
hints: First find the working stress: the force in newtons divided by the area.
The factor of safety is the yield stress divided by the working stress.
Divide 250 by the working stress in MPa.
questions.onCorrect: 2.5: the working stress is 100 MPa, and 250 ÷ 100 is the factor of safety.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the working stress. The factor of safety compares it with the yield stress.
That is the working stress divided by the yield stress, upside down. A safe member has a factor above one.

questions.prompt: A steel tie must carry 60 kN. The steel yields at 250 MPa, and a factor of safety of 2 is required. Find the smallest cross-sectional area the tie may have, in mm².
hints: Find the allowable stress first: the yield stress divided by the factor of safety.
The smallest area is the force in newtons divided by the allowable stress.
Divide 60,000 by the allowable stress in MPa.
questions.onCorrect: 480 mm²: the allowable stress is 125 MPa, and 60,000 N over 125 MPa is the area.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the factor of safety instead of dividing. The allowable stress is lower than the yield stress.
That ignores the factor of safety. Divide the yield stress by it first.

questions.prompt: Square steel bars come with sides of 20, 25 and 30 mm. Which side length, in mm, is the smallest that gives an area of at least 480 mm²?
hints: Work out the area of each bar by multiplying its side by itself.
Reject any bar whose area is below 480 mm².
Of the bars that remain, pick the smallest.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Areas are 20 × 20 = 400, 25 × 25 = 625 and 30 × 30 = 900 mm². 400 mm² is too small, so the 25 mm bar is the lightest that works.

questions.onCorrect: 25 mm: the areas are 400, 625 and 900 mm², and 625 mm² is the smallest that is large enough.

misconceptions.feedback: That bar has an area of only 400 mm², below the minimum, so it would be overstressed.
That bar is large enough, but heavier than it needs to be. The smallest bar that works is the right choice.

questions.prompt: A 25 mm square steel tie, with a cross-section of 625 mm², is 3 m long and carries 60 kN. With E = 200 GPa, find its stretch, in mm.
hints: Find the stress first: 60,000 N divided by 625 mm².
The strain is the stress divided by E, with E in MPa, and the stretch is the strain times the length in mm.
Multiply the strain by 3,000 mm.
questions.onCorrect: 1.44 mm: a stress of 96 MPa gives a strain of 96/200,000 over 3,000 mm.

misconceptions.feedback: Check E: use 200,000 MPa and not 200.
That is the stress in MPa. Divide by E and multiply by the length to get a stretch.

questions.prompt: A steel with a yield stress of 355 MPa is used with a factor of safety of 2.5. Find the allowable working stress, in MPa.
hints: The allowable stress is below the yield stress, by the factor of safety.
Divide the yield stress by the factor of safety.
Divide 355 by 2.5.
questions.onCorrect: 142 MPa: the yield stress divided by the factor of safety.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the factor of safety. The allowable stress lies below the yield stress, so divide.

questions.prompt: A bar of steel with a cross-section of 300 mm² yields at 250 MPa and must keep a factor of safety of 1.5. Find the largest axial load it may carry, in kN.
hints: Find the allowable stress first: the yield stress divided by the factor of safety.
The largest load is the allowable stress times the area, which gives newtons.
Convert your answer from newtons to kilonewtons.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Allowable stress = 250 ÷ 1.5 MPa; load = 300 × 250 ÷ 1.5 = 50,000 N = 50 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 50 kN: an allowable stress of 250 ÷ 1.5 MPa acting on 300 mm².

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores the factor of safety. The allowable stress is the yield stress divided by it.
That is the load in newtons. The answer is wanted in kilonewtons.

questions.prompt: A 6 m beam on end supports carries 12 kN at 2 m from the left end, so the reactions are 8 kN at A and 4 kN at B. Find the shear force just to the right of the load, in kN, counting upward forces on the left piece as positive.
hints: Draw the piece to the left of a cut just past the load.
Both the 8 kN reaction and the 12 kN load are now on that piece, and one acts down.
Add the upward 8 kN and the downward 12 kN, with up positive.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Left of the cut: +8 kN reaction and −12 kN load, so V = 8 − 12 = −4 kN.

questions.onCorrect: −4 kN: the load is now on the left piece, so 8 − 12 leaves the shear negative.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign. The load is downward, so just to its right the upward forces on the left piece are outweighed.
That is the shear just to the left of the load. Just to its right, the load is on the left piece too.

questions.prompt: Bending moment (kN·m)
hints: Only the left reaction is on the left piece.
Multiply that force by its distance from the cut.
Calculate 8 × 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only RA acts left of the cut: M = 8 × 2 = 16 kN·m, sagging.

questions.onCorrect: 16 kN·m: the left reaction times its distance. The crate itself acts at the cut, so it adds no moment.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the reaction, not a moment. Multiply it by its distance from the cut.
That uses the crate's weight, but the crate acts at the cut and adds no moment.

questions.prompt: An 8 m beam on end supports carries a uniform 3 kN/m along its full length. Find the largest bending moment, in kN·m.
hints: The supports share the load equally, and the shear is zero at midspan.
Each reaction is half of the total load, and the load to the left of midspan acts at the middle of that half.
Or use wL²/8, with w = 3 and L = 8.
questions.onCorrect: 24 kN·m at midspan: wL²/8 = 3 × 64 ÷ 8.

misconceptions.feedback: That is wL² without dividing by eight.
That is each reaction, a force. The peak moment multiplies forces by distances.

questions.prompt: Along a simply supported beam, what is the shear force at the section where the bending moment reaches its peak?
hints: The shear is the slope of the bending moment diagram.
At the top of a hump the curve is neither rising nor falling.
Which value of the shear means a level slope?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Zero: the moment's slope is the shear, and the slope vanishes at the peak.

choices.label: Half the total load on the beam
The largest shear anywhere on the beam
Zero

questions.onCorrect: Zero: the moment stops rising and starts to fall at that section, so its slope, the shear, passes through zero.

misconceptions.feedback: The shear is the slope of the moment diagram, and at the top of a hump the curve is neither rising nor falling, so its slope there is zero rather than largest.
Half the load is the shear near a support when a single load sits at midspan. At the peak of the moment the curve is level, and the shear is its slope, which is zero.

questions.prompt: A 3 m cantilever carries a 5 kN load at its free end. Find the size of the bending moment at the wall, in kN·m.
hints: Keep the piece away from the wall, since no reaction acts on it.
The only force on that piece is the 5 kN load, acting 3 m from the wall.
The moment is the force times its distance from the wall.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The load acts 3 m from the wall: M = 5 × 3 = 15 kN·m, hogging.

questions.onCorrect: 15 kN·m, hogging: the load acts 3 m from the wall, so M = 5 × 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the force. Multiply it by its distance from the wall to get a moment.
That adds the force and the distance. A moment multiplies them.

questions.prompt: A 10 m beam on end supports carries 20 kN at midspan. Find the largest bending moment, in kN·m.
hints: The load is at midspan, so each support carries half of it.
The largest moment is under the load, where the shear changes sign.
Multiply one reaction by its distance from the load, 5 m.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each reaction is 10 kN; under the load M = 10 × 5 = 50 kN·m. This is PL/4.

questions.onCorrect: 50 kN·m: a 10 kN reaction acting 5 m from the load, which is PL/4.

misconceptions.feedback: That is each reaction, a force. Multiply it by its distance from the load to get a moment.
That multiplies the reaction by the whole span. The distance from the support to the load is half of it.

questions.prompt: A solid rectangular beam 100 mm wide and 200 mm deep carries a bending moment of 20 kN·m. Its second moment of area is bh³/12. Find the largest bending stress, in MPa.
hints: Work out I from bh³/12, and take y as half the depth.
Write the moment in N·mm, which is 20 × 10⁶, then use σ = M y ÷ I.
questions.onCorrect: 30 MPa: the outer fibre is 100 mm from the neutral axis, in a section with I = 66.67 × 10⁶ mm⁴.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the full depth, 200 mm, for y. The outer fibre is half the depth from the neutral axis.

questions.prompt: The same 20 kN·m acts on the same section laid flat, so that it is 200 mm wide and 100 mm deep. Find the largest bending stress, in MPa.
hints: Laid flat, the depth is 100 mm, so y is half of that.
I = bh³/12 with b = 200 mm and h = 100 mm.
Calculate 20 × 10⁶ × 50 ÷ I.
questions.onCorrect: 60 MPa, twice as much as on edge: the shallower section has a much smaller I and an outer fibre closer in.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the stress with the beam on edge. Laid flat, I is much smaller.
That keeps y at the old 100 mm. Laid flat, the depth is 100 mm, so y is half of that.

questions.prompt: Find the second moment of area of a rectangle 60 mm wide and 100 mm deep, about its horizontal centroidal axis, in units of 10⁶ mm⁴.
hints: For a rectangle, I = bh³/12, with the depth cubed.
Cube 100 mm first, then multiply by 60 and divide by 12.
Give the answer in units of 10⁶ mm⁴.

misconceptions.feedback: That is I in mm⁴. The question asks in units of 10⁶ mm⁴, so divide by 10⁶.

questions.prompt: An I-section is 200 mm deep and 100 mm wide, with flanges 10 mm thick and a web 6 mm thick. Treat it as the outer rectangle minus the two empty regions beside the web. Find its second moment of area, in units of 10⁶ mm⁴, to two decimal places.
hints: The empty regions together are a rectangle as deep as the space between the flanges, 200 − 2 × 10 mm, and as wide as 100 − 6 mm.
Work out each cube first, subtract, divide by 12 and give the answer in units of 10⁶ mm⁴.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 × 200³ = 800 × 10⁶ and 94 × 180³ = 548.2 × 10⁶; the difference over 12 is 20.98 × 10⁶ mm⁴.

questions.onCorrect: 20.98 × 10⁶ mm⁴: the outer rectangle gives 800 × 10⁶ and the empty regions take away 548.2 × 10⁶ before dividing by 12.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the solid rectangle, 100 mm by 200 mm. Subtract the empty regions beside the web first.
That is the difference of the two products before the division by twelve.

questions.prompt: A square beam 100 mm × 100 mm carries a bending moment of 5 kN·m. Find the largest bending stress, in MPa.
hints: I = bh³/12, and y is half the depth.
Write the moment in N·mm, which is 5 × 10⁶.
questions.onCorrect: 30 MPa: I = 8.33 × 10⁶ mm⁴ and the outer fibre is 50 mm from the neutral axis.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the full depth for y. The outer fibre is half the depth from the neutral axis.

questions.prompt: Name the line through a bent beam's cross-section along which the material is neither squeezed nor stretched.
hints: It is the layer that neither shortens nor lengthens as the beam bends.
In a symmetric section it runs through the middle of the depth.
The name has two words, and the second one says what kind of line it is.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The neutral axis, which passes through the centroid of the section.

questions.onCorrect: The neutral axis: the layer between the squeezed side and the stretched side.

misconceptions.feedback: That line does sit in the middle, but it has a specific name. What do engineers call the line of zero bending stress?

questions.prompt: A steel cantilever 2 m long (E = 200 GPa, I = 2 × 10⁶ mm⁴) carries 3 kN at its tip. Using δ = PL³/3EI, find the tip deflection in mm.
hints: Convert to N, m, Pa and m⁴: 10⁶ mm⁴ is 10⁻⁶ m⁴.
Compute EI first, then PL³/3EI in metres.
Calculate 3,000 × 2³ ÷ (3 × 400,000), then convert to mm.
questions.onCorrect: 20 mm: base units throughout, then metres converted to millimetres.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the deflection in metres. Convert it to mm.
That leaves out the 3 in the denominator, 3EI.

questions.prompt: A cantilever keeps the same load and section, but its length is doubled. By what factor does its tip deflection grow?
hints: In δ = PL³ ÷ 3EI, only the length changes.
The length appears cubed.
Replace L by 2L and see what multiplies the result.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: δ ∝ L³, so doubling L multiplies δ by 2³ = 8.

questions.onCorrect: 8: the length is cubed, so doubling it gives 2³.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by 3. Cubing means 2 × 2 × 2.
That is the factor for doubling the load. The length is cubed.
That squares the length. In PL³ ÷ 3EI it is cubed.

questions.prompt: An aluminium cantilever (E = 70 GPa) has I = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴ and is 1 m long, with a 2.1 kN load at its tip. Find the tip deflection, in mm.
hints: Write every quantity in base units: the load is 2,100 N and E is 70 × 10⁹ Pa.
EI = 70 × 10⁹ × 1 × 10⁻⁶ N·m², and δ = PL³ ÷ 3EI comes out in metres.
Convert the deflection from metres to millimetres.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the deflection in metres. The question asks in millimetres, so multiply by 1,000.

questions.prompt: For a 2 m steel cantilever (E = 200 GPa, I = 2 × 10⁶ mm⁴), find the tip stiffness k = 3EI ÷ L³, in kN/m.
hints: Divide 3EI by L³, with L = 2 m.
Convert from N/m to kN/m.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the stiffness in N/m. The question wants kN/m.
That leaves out the 3 in 3EI ÷ L³.

questions.prompt: A 2 m steel cantilever (E = 200 GPa) carries 3 kN at its tip, and its deflection is limited to 8 mm. Find the smallest second moment of area it may have, in units of 10⁶ mm⁴.
hints: Rearrange δ = PL³ ÷ 3EI to give I = PL³ ÷ 3Eδ.
Use base units: P = 3,000 N, L = 2 m, E = 200 × 10⁹ Pa, δ = 0.008 m.
The answer in m⁴ is multiplied by 10¹² to give mm⁴, or by 10⁶ to give units of 10⁶ mm⁴.

misconceptions.feedback: That is I in mm⁴. The question asks in units of 10⁶ mm⁴.

questions.prompt: Which single change halves a cantilever's tip deflection under the same load?
hints: Look at where each quantity sits in δ = PL³ ÷ 3EI.
A change that halves the deflection has to enlarge something in the denominator.

acceptedIdeas: Doubling the second moment of area
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Doubling the second moment of area. δ = PL³/3EI, so doubling I halves δ.

choices.label: Doubling the length
Doubling the second moment of area
Halving Young's modulus

questions.onCorrect: Doubling I doubles the denominator, which halves the deflection.

misconceptions.feedback: The length sits on top and is cubed, so doubling it makes the deflection much larger.
E is in the denominator, so halving it doubles the deflection.

questions.prompt: A crowbar is levered over a fulcrum. The hand pushes 1.2 m from the fulcrum and the load sits 0.2 m from it. Find the mechanical advantage.
hints: The mechanical advantage of a lever is the effort arm divided by the load arm.
The effort arm is the distance from the fulcrum to the hand.
Divide 1.2 by 0.2.
questions.onCorrect: 6: the effort arm is six times as long as the load arm.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the arms. Mechanical advantage is a ratio of the two.
That is the ratio upside down. Here the effort arm is the longer one.

questions.prompt: A crowbar's hand end is 1.2 m from the fulcrum and its load, 900 N, is 0.2 m from it. Find the effort, in N.
hints: Balance the moments about the fulcrum: effort times its arm equals load times its arm.
The effort is the unknown, with an arm of 1.2 m.
Divide 900 × 0.2 by 1.2.
questions.onCorrect: 150 N: 900 × 0.2 ÷ 1.2, which is the load divided by the mechanical advantage of 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the mechanical advantage. A lever reduces the effort that is needed.
That is the load. The effort is smaller, because the long arm helps.

questions.prompt: A pulley system has 4 rope strands supporting the moving block, which carries an 800 N load. Ignoring friction and the weight of the block, find the effort, in N.
hints: The supporting strands share the load equally.
Each strand carries the load divided by the number of strands.
The effort is the tension in one strand.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the 4 strands carries the rope tension: effort = 800 ÷ 4 = 200 N.

questions.onCorrect: 200 N: the four strands share the 800 N, and the pull on the free end equals the tension in one.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the number of strands. They share the load, so divide.
That is the load, not the effort. The strands share it.

questions.prompt: To lift an 800 N load by 0.5 m with 4 supporting strands, how many metres of rope must be pulled through?
hints: When the block rises 0.5 m, each supporting strand has to get shorter by 0.5 m.
That shortening is taken from the rope at the free end.
Add the shortening of all four strands.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each strand shortens by 0.5 m: 4 × 0.5 = 2 m.

questions.onCorrect: 2 m: each of the 4 strands shortens by 0.5 m.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides. Every strand shortens by the lift, so multiply by the number of strands.
That is the lift. The rope pulled through is more than that, since each strand shortens.

questions.prompt: In the forearm, the biceps attaches 0.04 m from the elbow, and a 50 N weight is held in the hand 0.32 m from the elbow. Treating the forearm as a weightless horizontal lever, find the biceps force, in N.
hints: The elbow is the fulcrum. Balance the moments of the biceps and of the weight about it.
The biceps force times 0.04 m equals the weight times 0.32 m.
Divide 50 × 0.32 by 0.04.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Biceps × 0.04 = 50 × 0.32, so the biceps pulls 16 ÷ 0.04 = 400 N, eight times the weight held.

questions.onCorrect: 400 N, eight times the weight: the effort arm is the shorter one, so the effort must be the larger force.
