answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The lever is held at rest, so its net moment is zero.. At rest the net moment is zero, so effort × effort arm equals load × load arm.

choices.label: The lever is held at rest, so its net moment is zero.
Because the two arms are always equal.
Because the effort always equals the load.

questions.onCorrect: A lever at rest has no net moment, so its clockwise and anticlockwise moments are equal.

misconceptions.feedback: The arms usually differ, and that difference is what gives the mechanical advantage.
The effort and the load differ too. Only their moments match.

questions.prompt: In tweezers, the effort is applied between the fulcrum and the load. Which class of lever is that?
hints: Which of the three points is in the middle?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Third class. Effort in the middle is a third-class lever.

choices.label: First class
Third class
Second class

questions.onCorrect: Effort in the middle makes a third-class lever, which gives up force for speed and reach.

misconceptions.feedback: First class has the fulcrum in the middle, like a seesaw.
Second class has the load in the middle, like a nutcracker.

questions.prompt: A pulley system has 3 rope strands supporting the moving block, which carries a 900 N load. Ignoring friction and the weight of the block, find the effort, in N.
hints: The supporting strands share the load equally.
Each strand carries the load divided by the number of strands.
The effort is the tension in one strand.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the 3 strands carries the rope tension: effort = 900 ÷ 3 = 300 N.

questions.onCorrect: 300 N: the three strands share the 900 N.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the number of strands. They share the load, so divide.
That is the load. The strands share it.

questions.prompt: A see-saw balances with a 300 N child sitting 2 m from the pivot on one side. The other child also sits 2 m from the pivot, on the other side. How heavy is that child, in newtons?
hints: Each sits the same distance from the middle.
What would tip the see-saw if the weights differed?
Equal distances need equal weights.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Equal distances from the pivot balance only if the weights are equal, so the other child also weighs 300 N.

questions.onCorrect: 300 N. At equal distances, equal moments need equal weights. Next: what if the distances differ?

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two weights. Balance needs the two sides to turn the see-saw equally.
Half the weight would only balance at twice the distance. Both children sit the same distance out.

questions.prompt: Which change doubles the moment of a push on a spanner?
hints: M = F × d. Which letter does each option change?

acceptedIdeas: Push at twice the distance from the bolt
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Push at twice the distance from the bolt. Doubling d doubles M = F × d.

choices.label: Push at twice the distance from the bolt
Push with half the force
Push along the handle instead of across it

questions.onCorrect: M = F × d, so doubling the perpendicular distance doubles the moment.

misconceptions.feedback: Half the force halves the moment. Moment is force times distance.
A push along the handle has no distance at right angles to it, so it does not turn the bolt.

questions.prompt: Why does only 90 sin 30° count towards the moment?
hints: Which part of the force could swing the handle round?

acceptedIdeas: Only the part of the force across the spanner turns it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only the part of the force across the spanner turns it.. The component along the spanner does not turn it; the component across it does.

choices.label: Sine is used for every moment, whatever the angle.
The bolt is only affected by the smaller part of any force.
Only the part of the force across the spanner turns it.

questions.onCorrect: The part along the handle has no turning effect. Only the part across it does.

misconceptions.feedback: A push at right angles needs no sine at all. Sine appears here because of the angle to the spanner.
Size is not the reason. The part along the handle is a real force but has no turning effect.

questions.prompt: A 60 N force acts on a 0.5 m wrench at 30° to the wrench. Find the moment about the nut, in N·m.
hints: Only the part of the force across the wrench turns it.
The part across the wrench is the force times the sine of the angle to the wrench.
Multiply 60 × sin 30° by the 0.5 m distance.
questions.onCorrect: 15 N·m: the across part is 60 sin 30°, and it acts 0.5 m from the nut.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the whole push as acting across the wrench. At 30° only part of it does.
That uses cos 30°, which is the part along the wrench. The part across it is the sine.

questions.prompt: A 6 m plank rests on a post at each end, with a 12 kN crate 2 m from the left end. The left post pushes up with 8 kN. Cut the plank 1 m from the left end. What downward force, in kN, must the cut face supply to keep the left piece still?
hints: Draw the left piece alone, 1 m long, and mark every force acting on it from outside.
The crate is 2 m from the left end, so it is beyond the cut and is not on the left piece.
The cut face must balance the one force that does act on the left piece.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the post's 8 kN acts on the left piece, so the cut face must supply 8 kN the other way.

questions.onCorrect: 8 kN: only the left post's push acts on the left piece, so the cut face must supply an equal force the other way.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole crate, which sits to the right of the cut and is not on the left piece.
That is the right post's push, which acts on the far piece.

questions.prompt: The left reaction is 10 kN upward and nothing else acts on the left piece. What is the shear force at the cut?
hints: Count upward forces on the left piece as positive.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: +10 kN. The only force is 10 kN upward, so V = +10 kN.

choices.label: +10 kN
0 kN
−10 kN

questions.onCorrect: Upward forces on the left piece count positive, so the shear is +10 kN.

misconceptions.feedback: An upward force on the left piece counts positive, so the sign is the other way.
The reaction is on the left piece and nothing cancels it, so the shear is not zero.

questions.prompt: A 5 kN upward force acts on the left piece, 2 m from the cut. Find its moment about the cut in kN·m.
hints: A moment is force times perpendicular distance.
The force is 5 kN and the distance is 2 m.
Multiply them.
questions.onCorrect: 10 kN·m. The bending moment adds up force times distance for every force on the piece.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the force and the distance. A moment multiplies them.
That divides the force by the distance. A moment multiplies them.

questions.prompt: Why is it enough to use only the forces on the left piece when finding the moment at a cut?
hints: Think about what is true of each piece of the beam taken on its own.
What would the right piece give?

acceptedIdeas: Each piece balances on its own, so either one gives the same moment.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each piece balances on its own, so either one gives the same moment.. Each piece is in equilibrium, so one side's forces give the whole moment.

choices.label: The left side of a beam is always the stronger side.
Forces to the right never produce a moment.
Each piece balances on its own, so either one gives the same moment.

questions.onCorrect: The whole beam is in equilibrium, so each piece balances on its own and either one gives the same moment.

misconceptions.feedback: Forces on the right do have moments about the cut. They give the same answer as the ones on the left.
Neither side is stronger. The beam is the same whichever piece is used.

questions.prompt: An 8 m beam on end supports carries 24 kN at 6 m from the left end, so the reactions are 6 kN at A and 18 kN at B. Find the shear force just to the right of the load, in kN, counting upward forces on the left piece as positive.
hints: Draw the piece to the left of a cut just past the load.
That piece holds the 6 kN reaction and the 24 kN load.
Add the upward 6 kN and the downward 24 kN, with up positive.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Left of the cut: +6 kN reaction and −24 kN load, so V = 6 − 24 = −18 kN, which matches B's reaction.

questions.onCorrect: −18 kN: 6 − 24, which matches the reaction at B acting on the other piece.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign. Just right of a downward load, the upward forces on the left piece are outweighed.
That is the shear just to the left of the load. Just to its right, the load is on the left piece too.

questions.prompt: A 20 kN load hangs from a single steel rod. You replace the rod with two identical rods side by side, sharing the load equally. What force, in kN, does each rod carry?
hints: The two rods share the load equally.
Together they carry the whole 20 kN.
Divide the load between the two rods.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two identical rods share the 20 kN equally, so each carries 20 ÷ 2 = 10 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 10 kN each. Each rod now carries half the force, but it is the force per area that matters.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole load on one rod. The two rods share it.
Two rods do not double the load. Together they carry exactly the load.

questions.prompt: A bar carries a fixed force. Its cross-sectional area is doubled. What happens to the stress?
hints: Stress is force divided by area.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It halves. σ = F/A, so doubling A halves σ.

choices.label: It stays the same
It doubles
It halves

questions.onCorrect: Stress is F/A, so doubling the area halves the stress for the same force.

misconceptions.feedback: Stress is force divided by area, so more area means less stress.
The force is the same, but it is spread over a larger area.

questions.prompt: A bar 2 m long stretches by 1 mm under load. Find its strain, as a plain number.
hints: Strain is the extension divided by the original length.
The extension and the length have to be in the same unit, so convert the 2 m to millimetres.
Divide 1 mm by the length in mm.
questions.onCorrect: 0.0005: 1 mm ÷ 2,000 mm. Strain is a ratio, so it carries no unit.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides 1 by 2 without converting. The extension is in millimetres, so the length has to be in millimetres too.
That is the length divided by the stretch, upside down. Strain is the stretch over the length.

questions.prompt: Why is E written as 200,000 MPa and not 200 GPa in this calculation?
hints: Look at the units of the stress that is divided by E.
What would the strain's unit be if the two units differed?

acceptedIdeas: Stress and E must share a unit, so that strain comes out as a plain ratio.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Stress and E must share a unit, so that strain comes out as a plain ratio.. Stress and E must share a unit, so 200 GPa becomes 200,000 MPa.

choices.label: Stress and E must share a unit, so that strain comes out as a plain ratio.
Because strain is measured in MPa.
Because MPa is the only unit allowed for E.

questions.onCorrect: Stress and E must be in the same unit, so that their ratio, the strain, comes out as a plain number.

misconceptions.feedback: E can be quoted in GPa. In this calculation it only has to match the unit of the stress.
Strain has no unit. It is the ratio of two lengths, or of two stresses.

questions.prompt: A steel bar (E = 200 GPa) is strained elastically to 0.0012. Find the stress in the bar, in MPa.
hints: In the elastic range, stress equals E times strain.
E has to be in MPa to give a stress in MPa.
Multiply 200,000 by 0.0012.
questions.onCorrect: 240 MPa: σ = Eε, with E = 200,000 MPa.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the stress in GPa, from using E = 200. E in MPa gives a stress in MPa.

questions.prompt: A 6 m plank is held up by a post at each end. A 12 kN crate sits exactly halfway along it. How much does each post carry, in kN?
hints: The crate is exactly halfway. Does either post carry more?
The two posts together must carry the whole crate.
Share the crate between the two equally.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The crate is at the middle, so by symmetry each post carries half of 12 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 6 kN each, by symmetry. What if the crate is nearer one end?

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole crate on one post. Symmetry shares it between the two.
That is only a quarter of the crate. The two posts together must carry all of it.

questions.prompt: You take moments about support A. Which unknown force disappears from the equation?
hints: Where does the reaction at A act? How far is that from A?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The reaction at A. The reaction at A passes through A, so its moment about A is zero.

choices.label: The reaction at B
The reaction at A
The load

questions.onCorrect: The reaction at A acts through A, so it has no arm and no moment about A.

misconceptions.feedback: The reaction at B acts at a distance from A, so it still has a moment about A.
The load is known, and it acts away from A, so it stays in the equation.

questions.prompt: Why take moments about the pin at A?
hints: Think about what happens to the moment of RA about A.
Which unknown would remain in the equation?

acceptedIdeas: The reaction at A acts through A, so it drops out and leaves one unknown.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The reaction at A acts through A, so it drops out and leaves one unknown.. The reaction at A passes through A, so it has no moment and drops out.

choices.label: The reaction at A acts through A, so it drops out and leaves one unknown.
The load always acts at A.
Moments can only be taken about the left support.

questions.onCorrect: A force acting through the pivot has no moment about it, so RA drops out and only RB is left.

misconceptions.feedback: Moments can be taken about any point. The skill is choosing the one that removes an unknown.
The loads here sit at 3 m and 6 m from A, not at A. The reason is about the reaction at A.

questions.prompt: A load of 5 kN/m covers 4 m of a beam, starting at its left end. Which single force replaces it when finding reactions?
hints: The size of the single force is the load per metre times the loaded length.
A uniform load acts at the middle of the length it covers.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 20 kN at x = 2 m. 5 × 4 = 20 kN, acting at the middle of the loaded length, x = 2 m.

choices.label: 5 kN at x = 2 m
20 kN at x = 2 m
20 kN at x = 4 m

questions.onCorrect: 20 kN at the middle of the loaded length: 5 kN/m over 4 m, acting 2 m from the end.

misconceptions.feedback: The force acts at the middle of the loaded length, 2 m from the end, and not at the far end of it.
That is the load per metre. The total is that times the loaded length.

questions.prompt: A 10 m beam rests on supports at its two ends and carries 3 kN/m over its whole length. Find the left reaction, in kN.
hints: The whole spread load is the load per metre times the length.
That load acts at the middle of the beam.
A load at the middle is shared equally by the two end supports.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The load totals 3 × 10 = 30 kN at the middle, so each support carries half: 15 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 15 kN: the load totals 30 kN at the middle, and each support carries half.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole load. Each support carries a share of it.
That is a quarter of the load. Each of the two supports carries half.

questions.prompt: A symmetrical triangular truss carries a 12 kN load at its apex and rests on two supports, one under each foot. What force, in kN, does each support carry?
hints: The truss is symmetrical and the load is at the middle.
Together the two supports carry the whole load.
Divide the load between the two supports.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The supports share the 12 kN load equally, so each carries 12 ÷ 2 = 6 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 6 kN each. A symmetrical load is shared equally between the supports.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole load on one support. The two supports share it.
Two supports do not double the load. Together they carry exactly the load.

questions.prompt: A rope holds up a hanging lamp. Is the rope in tension or compression?
hints: Is the rope being stretched or squashed?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Tension. The rope is stretched along its length, so it is in tension.

choices.label: Compression
Tension

questions.onCorrect: The rope is pulled along its length, so it is in tension. A member that is pushed is in compression.

misconceptions.feedback: Compression squashes a member. A rope that holds something up is being stretched.

questions.prompt: Why is there a factor of 2 in 2 × F × 2.5/6.5 = 10?
hints: Count the members that meet at the apex.
Each of them contributes a vertical part to carry the load.

acceptedIdeas: Two sloping members meet at the apex and each gives an equal vertical part.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two sloping members meet at the apex and each gives an equal vertical part.. Two members meet at the apex, each giving a vertical part of F × 4/5.

choices.label: Each member carries double its own vertical part.
The load is counted twice, once for each support.
Two sloping members meet at the apex and each gives an equal vertical part.

questions.onCorrect: Two sloping members meet at the apex, and each gives an equal vertical part.

misconceptions.feedback: The load is counted once. The 2 counts the members meeting at the joint.
A member's vertical part is its force times rise over length. It is not doubled.

questions.prompt: A triangular truss spans 6 m, with its apex 4 m above the supports, so each sloping member is 5 m long. A 32 kN load hangs at the apex. Find the force in each sloping member, in kN.
hints: Isolate the apex, where the two sloping members and the load meet.
Each sloping member's vertical part is its force times 4/5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At the apex 2F × 4/5 = 32, so F = 32 ÷ 1.6 = 20 kN.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole load. Two members share it, and each is slanted.
That is each member's vertical part. The member itself carries more, because it slants.

questions.prompt: A trolley on a straight rail is pulled by 15 kN to the right through one rope and 6 kN to the left through another. Find the size of the resultant pull, in kN.
hints: The two ropes pull along one line but in opposite directions.
Call right positive, so the leftward pull counts as negative.
Add the two signed pulls.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Taking right as positive, the resultant is 15 + (−6) = 9 kN to the right.

questions.onCorrect: 9 kN to the right: the 6 kN pull cancels part of the 15 kN, and the sign of each force follows its direction.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two sizes, which is right only when both ropes pull the same way. These pull against each other.
That multiplies the sizes. Forces on one line combine by adding or subtracting, with direction deciding which.

questions.prompt: A brace carries a 15 kN pull along a line that rises 3 for every 4 across. Find the vertical component of the pull, in kN.
hints: The slope triangle with sides 3 and 4 has a sloping side of 5.
The vertical share of the force is the rise divided by the sloping side.
Multiply the 15 kN force by that share.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sloping side is √(3² + 4²) = 5, so the vertical share is 3/5 and the vertical component is 15 × 3/5 = 9 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 9 kN: the force times rise over sloping side, 15 × 3/5.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the horizontal component, the force times run over sloping side. The vertical component uses the rise.
That is the rise of the triangle, not a force. The component is the force times the share 3/5.
That divides the rise by the run instead of by the sloping side. The share is measured against the full length of the slope.

questions.prompt: A ring is pulled straight up by a 9 kN cable and by a second 10 kN cable that rises 3 for every 4 across. Find the size of the resultant of the two pulls, in kN.
hints: Split the slanted cable into a horizontal and a vertical component first.
The slanted cable gives 10 × 4/5 across and 10 × 3/5 up. Add its vertical part to the 9 kN.
Combine the horizontal total and the vertical total with Pythagoras.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The slanted cable gives 8 kN across and 6 kN up. The vertical total is 9 + 6 = 15 kN, so R = √(8² + 15²) = √289 = 17 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 17 kN: 8 kN across and 15 kN up, which combine as √(8² + 15²).

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two cable forces as sizes. They do not act on one line, so their components have to be combined instead.
That is the vertical total alone. The slanted cable also pulls the ring sideways, and the 8 kN across has to be included.
That swaps the horizontal and vertical parts of the slanted cable. The vertical part uses the rise, 3/5 of the force, and the horizontal part uses the run.

questions.prompt: A cable pulls with 40 kN at 25° above the horizontal. Find the vertical component of the pull, in kN, to one decimal place.
hints: The vertical side is opposite the 25° angle.
The side opposite the angle takes the sine, so the share is F sin θ.
Calculate 40 × sin 25° with the calculator in degrees mode.
questions.onCorrect: 16.9 kN: the side opposite the angle takes the sine, so 40 sin 25°.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 40 cos 25°, the horizontal part. The vertical side is opposite the angle, so it takes the sine.
That is the whole force. Only a share of it acts upward.

questions.prompt: Why does the moment of the 80 N push use 80 sin 40° and not the full 80 N?
hints: Think about the two components of the push, along the spanner and across it.
Which of the two can turn the spanner about the bolt?

acceptedIdeas: Only the part of the push across the spanner turns it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only the part of the push across the spanner turns it.

choices.label: Only the part of the push across the spanner turns it.
Part of the push is lost to friction in the nut.
The sine turns a force in newtons into a moment in newton metres.

questions.onCorrect: The part along the handle only presses on the bolt. The part across the handle is the one that turns it.

misconceptions.feedback: The distance turns newtons into newton metres, not the sine. The sine only picks out the part of the force that lies across the spanner.
Friction is not the reason, and the part along the handle is not lost. It simply has no turning effect.

questions.prompt: A nut will not turn until the moment on it reaches 36 N·m. A mechanic pushes at the end of a 0.6 m spanner, at 30° to the handle. What force is needed, in N?
hints: The moment must be 36 N·m, so work backwards from it.
The moment is the across-part of the push, F sin 30°, times 0.6 m.
Divide 36 by (0.6 × sin 30°).
questions.onCorrect: 120 N: only half of the push, F sin 30°, acts across the handle, so the push is twice what a right-angled one would need.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 36 ÷ 0.6, the force for a push at right angles. At 30° only part of the push acts across the handle, so more is needed.
That divides by cos 30°, the part along the handle. The part across the spanner is the sine.

questions.prompt: A 360 N child sits 2.5 m to the left of a see-saw's pivot. How far to the right of the pivot, in metres, must a 450 N child sit for the see-saw to balance?
hints: Balance means the anticlockwise moment equals the clockwise moment.
The left moment is 360 × 2.5, and the right moment is 450 times the unknown distance.
Set the two equal and divide by 450.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Left moment = 360 × 2.5 = 900 N·m, so 450d = 900 and d = 2 m.

questions.onCorrect: 2 m: 450 × 2 = 900 N·m, which equals 360 × 2.5.

misconceptions.feedback: Equal distances balance only equal weights. The heavier child must sit nearer the pivot.
That divides by the wrong weight. The left moment, 900 N·m, is divided by the right child's weight.

questions.prompt: A 7 m beam rests on supports at 0 and at 5 m from its left end, and carries a 10 kN load at its free right-hand end. Find the reaction at the support 5 m from the left end, in kN.
hints: Take moments about the support at 0, so that its reaction drops out.
The load is 7 m from that support and the other support is 5 m from it.
Solve 5 × R = 10 × 7.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: About the support at 0: 5R = 10 × 7 = 70, so R = 14 kN, which is more than the 10 kN load.

questions.onCorrect: 14 kN, more than the whole load, because the support at 0 is pulling down 4 kN.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the load itself. The reaction is larger, because the load sits beyond the support and levers against the other one.
That is the size of the other reaction, which acts downward. The support asked about carries the larger force.
That is the distance of the load from the first support, not a force. The moment equation, 5R = 10 × 7, gives the reaction.

questions.prompt: An 8 m beam rests on a pin at its left end A and a roller at its right end B. It carries 2 kN/m over its left 4 m and a 12 kN point load 6 m from A. Find the reaction at B, in kN.
hints: Replace the spread load by a single force at the middle of its length first.
The spread load is 8 kN acting 2 m from A, and the point load is 12 kN at 6 m. Take moments about A.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The spread load is 2 × 4 = 8 kN at 2 m from A. About A: 8RB = 8 × 2 + 12 × 6 = 88, so RB = 11 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 11 kN: 8RB = 16 + 72, with the spread load counted as 8 kN at 2 m.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the reaction at A. The question asks for the roller at B.
That puts the spread load's 8 kN at the end of its length, 4 m from A. It acts at the middle, 2 m from A.
That shares the 20 kN of load equally. The loads are not at the middle of the beam, so the supports do not share it equally.

questions.prompt: A 6 m beam rests on supports at its two ends and carries a single 21 kN load 4 m from its left end. Find the left reaction, in kN.
hints: Take moments about the right-hand support, so that the left reaction is the only unknown.
The load is 2 m from the right-hand support.
Solve 6 × RA = 21 × 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: About the right-hand support: 6RA = 21 × 2 = 42, so RA = 7 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 7 kN: the load is nearer the right-hand support, so the left one carries the smaller share.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the right-hand reaction, the support nearer the load. The question asks for the left one.
That shares the load equally, but the load is not at the middle of the beam.

questions.prompt: A triangular roof truss spans 30 m, with its apex 8 m above the supports, so each sloping member is 17 m long. A 48 kN load hangs at the apex. Find the tension in the bottom member, in kN.
hints: Work at the apex first: the two sloping members share the load, and each has a vertical part of F × 8/17.
Then at a foot, the bottom member balances the horizontal part of the sloping member, F × 15/17.
Solve 2 × F × 8/17 = 48 for F, then multiply by 15/17.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At the apex 2F × 8/17 = 48, so F = 51 kN in each sloping member. At a foot the bottom member balances the horizontal part: 51 × 15/17 = 45 kN, in tension.

questions.onCorrect: 45 kN, in tension: each sloping member carries 51 kN, and 15/17 of that acts along the bottom.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the force in each sloping member. The bottom member balances only its horizontal part.
That is the vertical part of a sloping member, which the support's reaction balances. The bottom member balances the horizontal part.
That is the load itself. The forces in the members follow from balancing joint by joint.

questions.prompt: A 36 kN load hangs equally from three identical steel rods, each with a cross-section of 120 mm². Find the stress in each rod, in MPa.
hints: Identical rods share the load equally, so find the force in one rod first.
Each rod carries the total divided by the number of rods. Convert that force to newtons.
Divide the force in one rod by its own cross-sectional area.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each rod carries 36 ÷ 3 = 12 kN, so σ = 12,000 N ÷ 120 mm² = 100 MPa.

questions.onCorrect: 100 MPa: each rod carries 12 kN, and 12,000 N over 120 mm² is 100 N/mm².

misconceptions.feedback: That puts the whole 36 kN on one rod. The three rods share it, so each carries a third.
That leaves the force in kilonewtons. Convert the 12 kN to newtons before dividing by the area in mm².

questions.prompt: A 36 kN load hangs equally from two identical aluminium rods (E = 70 GPa), each 1.4 m long with a cross-section of 100 mm². Find the stretch of each rod, in mm.
hints: The two rods share the load, so find the force in one rod and then its stress.
The strain is the stress divided by E, with E in MPa, and the stretch is the strain times the length in mm.
Each rod has 18,000 N on 100 mm². Divide that stress by 70,000, then multiply by 1,400.
questions.onCorrect: 3.6 mm: 180 MPa in each rod gives a strain of 180/70,000 over 1,400 mm.

misconceptions.feedback: That puts the whole 36 kN on one rod. The two rods share it, so each carries 18 kN.
E has to be in MPa to match the stress: 70 GPa is 70,000 MPa, not 70.

questions.prompt: A load of 84 kN is shared equally by two identical steel rods. The steel yields at 280 MPa and a factor of safety of 2.5 is required. Find the smallest cross-sectional area each rod may have, in mm².
hints: Each rod carries half of the load, so find the force in one rod first.
The allowable stress is the yield stress divided by the factor of safety.
Divide the force in one rod, in newtons, by the allowable stress.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each rod carries 42 kN. The allowable stress is 280 ÷ 2.5 = 112 MPa, so A = 42,000 ÷ 112 = 375 mm².

questions.onCorrect: 375 mm²: each rod carries 42 kN, and the allowable stress of 112 MPa gives its area.

misconceptions.feedback: That puts the whole 84 kN on one rod. The two rods share it, so each carries half.
That leaves out the factor of safety. The allowable stress is the yield stress divided by it.
That leaves out both the sharing and the factor of safety. Each rod carries half of the load, and the stress is held below the yield stress by the factor.

questions.prompt: A 12 m beam rests on supports at its two ends and carries a 36 kN load 8 m from the left end. Find the bending moment at a cut 9 m from the left end, in kN·m.
hints: Find the left reaction first, by moments about the right-hand support.
The left piece, 9 m long, now holds the left reaction and the 36 kN load, which is 1 m from the cut.
Take moments about the cut: the reaction times 9 m, minus the load times 1 m.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: RA = 36 × 4 ÷ 12 = 12 kN. About the cut: M = 12 × 9 − 36 × 1 = 108 − 36 = 72 kN·m. The right piece gives 24 × 3 = 72 kN·m.

questions.onCorrect: 72 kN·m: 12 kN acts 9 m from the cut and the load acts 1 m from it the other way.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the left reaction's moment alone. The load is on the left piece too, and it turns the piece the other way.
That is the moment under the load, 8 m from the left end. The cut is 1 m beyond it.

questions.prompt: A 6 m cantilever carries a uniform load of 2 kN/m along its full length. Find the size of the bending moment at the wall, in kN·m.
hints: Replace the spread load by one force, as in the lesson on beam reactions.
The force acts at the middle of the loaded length, which is 3 m from the wall.
The moment is that force times 3 m.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The load is 2 × 6 = 12 kN, acting 3 m from the wall, so M = 12 × 3 = 36 kN·m, hogging.

questions.onCorrect: 36 kN·m, hogging: a 12 kN resultant acting 3 m from the wall.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total load, a force. The moment multiplies it by its distance from the wall.
That puts the 12 kN at the free end, 6 m away. A uniform load acts at the middle of its length.

questions.prompt: A rectangular beam 100 mm wide must carry a bending moment of 9.6 kN·m with a bending stress of no more than 160 MPa. Find the smallest depth it can have, in mm.
hints: Write the largest stress with I = bh³/12 and y = h/2, and set it equal to 160 MPa.
The largest stress simplifies to 6M ÷ (b × h²), with M in N·mm.
questions.onCorrect: 60 mm: the stress 6M ÷ (bh²) equals 160 MPa at that depth, and a deeper beam would have less.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes y as the full depth. The outer fibre is half the depth from the neutral axis.
That is the value of h². Take the square root to get the depth.

questions.prompt: A symmetric I-section 150 mm deep has a second moment of area of 10 × 10⁶ mm⁴. Find the largest bending stress under a moment of 6 kN·m, in MPa.
hints: The section is symmetric, so the outer fibre is half the depth from the neutral axis.
Write the moment in N·mm, which is 6 × 10⁶.
Calculate 6 × 10⁶ × 75 ÷ (10 × 10⁶).
questions.onCorrect: 45 MPa: the outer fibre is 75 mm from the neutral axis.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the full depth, 150 mm, for y. The outer fibre is half the depth from the neutral axis.
That leaves the moment in kN·m. Write it in N·mm, a factor of 10⁶ larger, to match mm and mm⁴.

questions.prompt: A rectangular steel cantilever (E = 200 GPa) is 2 m long, 50 mm wide and 100 mm deep, and carries 2 kN at its tip. Find the tip deflection, in mm.
hints: Find I first, from bh³ ÷ 12 with the depth as h, in mm⁴ and then in m⁴.
I = 50 × 100³ ÷ 12 = 4.167 × 10⁶ mm⁴, which is 4.167 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴. Then work out EI in N·m².
Calculate δ = 2,000 × 2³ ÷ (3 × EI) in metres, and convert to mm.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes the 50 mm as the depth. The depth, 100 mm, is the side that is cubed, so the section is stiffer than that.
That is the deflection in metres. The question asks in millimetres.

questions.prompt: A pulley system with 6 supporting strands raises a 960 N load by 0.75 m. Ignoring friction, find the work done by the effort, in J.
hints: The effort is the load divided by the number of strands.
The rope pulled through is the number of strands times the lift.
Work is the effort times the length of rope pulled through.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Effort = 960 ÷ 6 = 160 N. Rope pulled = 6 × 0.75 = 4.5 m. Work = 160 × 4.5 = 720 J, which equals 960 × 0.75.

questions.onCorrect: 720 J: 160 N through 4.5 m, which is exactly the load times the lift.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the effort, a force. Work is the effort times the distance it moves through.
That is the length of rope pulled through. Multiply it by the effort to get the work.
That multiplies the load by the number of strands and the lift. The effort is the load divided by the strands, not multiplied.

questions.prompt: A lever has an effort arm of 1.8 m and a load arm of 0.45 m. What load, in N, can an effort of 250 N hold?
hints: Balance the moments about the fulcrum: effort times its arm equals load times its arm.
The load is the effort times the ratio of the arms.
Multiply 250 by 1.8 and divide by 0.45.
questions.onCorrect: 1,000 N: the mechanical advantage is 1.8 ÷ 0.45 = 4, so the load is four times the effort.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the effort divided by the mechanical advantage. The load is larger than the effort, because the effort arm is the longer one.
That is the mechanical advantage. The load is the effort multiplied by it.

questions.prompt: A compound train has a 20-tooth gear driving a 40-tooth gear and, on the same shaft, a 15-tooth gear driving a 60-tooth gear. The input shaft turns at 2,400 rpm and carries 5 N·m. Ignoring losses, find the torque on the output shaft, in N·m.
hints: Find the ratio of each pair, and multiply them for the whole train.
The two ratios are 40 ÷ 20 and 60 ÷ 15.
Multiply the input torque by the overall ratio.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The ratios are 40 ÷ 20 = 2 and 60 ÷ 15 = 4, so the overall ratio is 8. The output speed is 2,400 ÷ 8 = 300 rpm, and the torque is 5 × 8 = 40 N·m.

questions.onCorrect: 40 N·m: the overall ratio is 2 × 4 = 8, and the lossless train multiplies the torque by it.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses only the first pair. A compound train has two, and their ratios multiply.
That uses only the second pair. A compound train has two, and their ratios multiply.

questions.prompt: A 36-tooth driver turning at 900 rpm meshes with a 12-tooth gear. Find the speed of the 12-tooth gear, in rpm.
hints: The same number of teeth pass the mesh each minute for both gears.
The driven gear has a third of the teeth, so it turns faster.
Calculate 900 × 36 ÷ 12.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The driven gear's speed is 900 × 36 ÷ 12 = 2,700 rpm.

questions.onCorrect: 2,700 rpm: the driven gear has a third of the teeth, so it turns three times as fast.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the ratio the wrong way round. A small driven gear turns faster than its driver.

questions.prompt: A winch is driven by a motor that delivers 10 N·m at 1,200 rpm. The drive from the motor to the hook is 75% efficient. What weight can it lift at a steady 0.6 m/s? Give the answer in N, to the nearest newton.
hints: Convert 1,200 rpm to radians per second, then find the motor's power as torque times angular speed.
Only 75% of the motor's power reaches the hook.
The force at the hook is the power there divided by the lifting speed.
questions.onCorrect: 1,571 N: the motor's 1,256.6 W becomes 942.5 W at the hook, and 942.5 ÷ 0.6 gives the force.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the efficiency. Only 75% of the motor's power reaches the hook.
That divides the motor's power by the efficiency. The hook receives less power than the motor delivers, so multiply.
That puts the rpm straight into the power. Convert the speed to radians per second first.

citations.claim: Forces acting along one line add when they point the same way and subtract when they point opposite ways.
Forces along one line combine by signed addition, so opposing pulls leave their difference.
A slanted force can be replaced by a horizontal and a vertical component; a force F at angle θ above the horizontal has components F cos θ and F sin θ.
A 20 kN force at 60° has components 20 cos 60° = 10 kN and 20 sin 60° = 17.32 kN, which reproduce the force by Pythagoras.
The horizontal component of a force at angle θ above the horizontal is F cos θ.
A force along a slope has components in the proportion of the slope triangle's sides: horizontal = F × run ÷ length, vertical = F × rise ÷ length.
On a 3-4-5 slope, the vertical share of a force is 3/5, so a 15 kN force has a 9 kN vertical component.
Perpendicular components combine as R = √(Rx² + Ry²); the rule for combining forces at a point goes back to Stevin (1586) and Newton's Principia (1687).
Forces of 3 kN and 4 kN at right angles have a resultant of 5 kN by Pythagoras.
A free-body diagram isolates one body and shows the forces acting on it; a body in static equilibrium has zero net force on it.
Only forces acting on the isolated body belong on its free-body diagram.
To keep a body in equilibrium the added force must equal the resultant of the others in size and oppose it in direction.
Resultant of several forces: add components in each direction, then combine the totals by Pythagoras.
Pulls of 15 kN and 6 kN in opposite directions along one line have a resultant of 9 kN.
The horizontal component of 10 kN at 30° is 10 cos 30° = 8.66 kN.
The side of the force triangle that touches the angle takes the cosine.
On a 3-4-5 slope, a 15 kN force has a vertical component of 15 × 3/5 = 9 kN.
The resultant of perpendicular forces of 3 kN and 4 kN is √(3² + 4²) = 5 kN.
The forces on a lamp's free-body diagram are its weight and the pulls of the cables on it.
The force balancing perpendicular forces of 6 kN and 8 kN is their 10 kN resultant reversed.
Components of the 10 kN cable on a 3-in-4 slope are 8 kN across and 6 kN up; with the 9 kN cable the resultant is √(8² + 15²) = 17 kN.
Perpendicular forces of 12 kN and 5 kN have a resultant of √(12² + 5²) = 13 kN.
On a 5-12-13 slope a 26 kN force has a vertical component of 26 × 5/13 = 10 kN.
The vertical component of 40 kN at 25° is 40 sin 25° = 16.9 kN.
The 5–12–13 triangle gives 13 × 12/13 = 12 kN.
R = √(9² + 12²) = 15 kN. The minus sign sets the direction, not the size.

citations.claim: The moment of a force about a pivot is the force times its perpendicular distance from the pivot, measured in newton metres.
A force at right angles to a door at distance d from the hinges has moment F × d about the hinges.
Only the component of a force perpendicular to the arm contributes to its moment: M = F d sin θ.
The moment equals the force times the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action; a force may slide along its line of action without changing its moment.
80 N at 40° on a lever arm of 0.35 m gives M = 80 × sin 40° × 0.35 ≈ 18.0 N·m.
The moment of a force at angle θ to the arm is F d sin θ.
A force whose line of action passes through the pivot has zero perpendicular distance and so zero moment.
A body in static equilibrium has zero net moment about any point, so clockwise and anticlockwise moments are equal; the law of the lever goes back to Archimedes.
For a see-saw in balance, the clockwise moment equals the anticlockwise moment about the pivot.
The moment of a force is greatest when it acts at the greatest distance from the pivot and at right angles to the arm.
A required moment fixes the force through M = F d sin θ, so a slanted push must be larger than a right-angled one.
A 40 N force at right angles, 0.8 m from the hinges, gives a moment of 32 N·m.
Only the component of the force perpendicular to the arm produces a moment.
60 N at 30° to a 0.5 m wrench gives M = 60 sin 30° × 0.5 = 15 N·m.
A force along the spanner has a line of action through the bolt and therefore no moment.
Balance needs 400 × d = 300 × 2 = 600 N·m, so d = 1.5 m.
Moment is greatest for a push at the far end of the handle at right angles to it.
A 36 N·m moment on a 0.6 m spanner at 30° needs F = 36 ÷ (0.6 sin 30°) = 120 N.
A 150 N force at right angles, 0.3 m from the bolt, has a moment of 45 N·m.
150 N at 30° to the handle, 0.3 m from the bolt, gives 150 sin 30° × 0.3 = 22.5 N·m.
Balance needs 450 × d = 360 × 2.5 = 900 N·m, so d = 2 m.
